## 18.7 Notes

Most of the concrete results above are standard. The general Theorem 18.8 and its extensions seem, however, to be new. For barrier options we refer to Rubinstein and Reiner (1991), and the survey in Carr (1995). Two standard papers on lookbacks are Come and Viswanathan (1991), and Goldman et al. (1979). See also Musiela and Rutkowski (1997). 

# STOCHASTIC OPTIMAL CONTROL

## 19.1 An Example

Let us consider an economic agent over a fixed time interval [0, TI. At time t = 0 the agent is endowed with initial wealth $\scriptstyle { \mathcal { X } } 0$ and his/her problem is how to allocate investments and consumption over the given time horizon. We assume that the agent's investment opportunities are the following: 

The agent can invest money in the bank at the deterministic short rate of interest $r ,$ i.e. he/she has access to the risk free asset B with 

$$
\mathrm{dB} = r B \mathrm{dt}.\tag{19.1}
$$

The agent can invest in a risky asset with price process $S _ { t }$ t, where we assume that the S-dynamics are given by a standard Black-Scholes model 

$$
\mathrm{d} S = \alpha S \mathrm{d} t + \sigma S \mathrm{d} W.\tag{19.2}
$$

We denote the agent's relative portfolio weights at time t by $\boldsymbol { u } _ { t } ^ { 0 }$ (for the riskless asset), and $u _ { t } ^ { 1 }$ (for the risky asset) respectively. His/her consumption rate at time t is denoted by $\pmb { c } _ { t }$ 

We restrict the consumer's investment-consumption strategies to be selffinancing, and as usual we assume that we live in a world where continuous trading and unlimited short selling is possible. If we denote the wealth of the consumer at time t by $X _ { t } ,$ it now follows from Lemma 6.4 that (after a slight rearrangement of terms) the X-dynamics are given by 

$$
\mathrm{d} X _ {t} = X _ {t} \left[ u _ {t} ^ {0} r + u _ {t} ^ {1} \alpha \right] \mathrm{dt} - c _ {t} \mathrm{dt} + u _ {t} ^ {1} \sigma X _ {t} \mathrm{d} W _ {t}.\tag{19.3}
$$

The object of the agent is to choose a portfolio-consumption strategy in such a way as to maximize &/her total utility over [0, T], and we assume that this utility is given by 

$$
E \left[ \int_ {0} ^ {T} F (t, c _ {t}) \mathrm{d} t + \Phi (X _ {T}) \right],\tag{19.4}
$$

where F is the instantaneous utility function for consumption, whereas $\Phi$ is a 4egacy" function which measures thp utility of having some money left at the end of the period. 

A natural constraint on consumption is the condition 

$$
c _ {t} \geq 0, \quad \forall t \geq 0,\tag{19.5}
$$

![image](https://cdn-mineru.openxlab.org.cn/result/2026-11-17/ec4b01e7-219e-4b27-ae7f-89d97615f591/04f0a69154258a5a3c59955d69efd7f471bcb0c8def8cbb1937483c85d4d4bf6.jpg)


and we also have of course the constraint 

$$
u _ {t} ^ {0} + u _ {t} ^ {1} = 1, \quad \forall t \geq 0.\tag{19.6}
$$

Depending upon the actual situation we may be forced to impose other constraints (it may, say, be natural to demand that the consumer's wealth never becomes negative), but we will not do this at the moment. 

We may now formally state the consumer's utility maximization problem as follows: 

$$
\max _ {u ^ {0}, u ^ {1}, c} E \left[ \int_ {0} ^ {T} F (t, c _ {t}) \mathrm{d} t + \Phi (X _ {T}) \right]\tag{19.7}
$$

èră 

$$
\mathrm{d} X _ {t} = X _ {t} \left[ u _ {t} ^ {0} r + u _ {t} ^ {1} \alpha \right] \mathrm{d} t - c _ {t} \mathrm{d} t + u _ {t} ^ {1} \sigma X _ {t} \mathrm{d} W _ {t},\tag{19.8}
$$

$$
X _ {0} = x _ {0},\tag{19.9}
$$

$$
c _ {t} \geq 0, \quad \forall t \geq 0,\tag{19.10}
$$

$$
u _ {t} ^ {0} + u _ {t} ^ {1} = 1, \quad \forall t \geq 0.\tag{19.11}
$$

A problem of this kind is known as a stochastic optimal control problem. In this context the process X is called the s t a t e process (or state variable), the processes $u ^ { 0 } , u ^ { 1 }$ , c are called control processes, and we have a number of control constraints. In the next sections we will study a fairly general class of stochastic optimal control problems. The method used is that of dynamic programming, and at the end of the chapter we will solve a version of the problem above. 

## 19.2 T h e Formal Problem

We now go on to study a fairly general class of optimal control problems. To this end, let $\mu ( t , { \bf x } , { \bf u } )$ and $\sigma ( t , \mathbf { x } , \mathbf { u } )$ be given functions of the form 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \mu : R _ {+} \times R ^ {n} \times R ^ {k} \to R ^ {n}, \\ \sigma : R _ {+} \times R ^ {n} \times R ^ {k} \to R ^ {n \times d}. \end{array}
$$

For a given point $\scriptstyle x _ { 0 } , \in \ R ^ { n }$ we will consider the following controlled stochastic differential equation: 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \mathrm{d} X _ {t} = \mu (t, X _ {t}, u _ {t}) \mathrm{d} t + \sigma (t, X _ {t}, u _ {t}) \mathrm{d} W _ {t}, \\ X _ {0} = x _ {0}. \end{array}\tag{19.12}
$$

(19.13) 

We view the n-dimensional process X as a s t a t e process, which we are trying to "control" (or "steer"). We can (partly) control the state process X by choosing the k-dimensional control process u in a suitable way. W is a d-dimensiona 

# THE FORMAL PROBLEM

Wiener process, and we must now try to give a precise mathematical meaning to the formal expressions (19.12)-(19.13). 

Remark 19.2.1 In this chapter, where we will work under a fixed measure, al Wiener processes are denoted by the letter W. 

Our first modeling problem concerns the class of admissible control processes. In most concrete cases it is natural to require that the control process u is adapted to the X process. In other words, at time t the value $\pmb { u } _ { t }$ of the control process is only allowed to "depend" on past observed values of the state process X. One natural way to obtain an adapted control process is by choosing a deterministic function ${ \boldsymbol g } ( t , { \boldsymbol x } )$ 

$$
g: R _ {+} \times R ^ {n} \rightarrow R ^ {k},
$$

and then defining the control process u by 

$$
\boldsymbol {u} _ {t} = g (t, X _ {t}).
$$

Such a function g is called a feedback control law, and in the sequel we will restrict ourselves to consider only feedback control laws. For mnemo-technical purposes we will often denote control laws by $\mathbf { u } ( t , \mathrm { x } )$ , rather than ${ \_ g } ( t , x )$ ), and write $u _ { t } = \mathbf { u } ( t , X _ { t } )$ . We use boldface in order to indicate that u is a function. In contrast to this we use the notation u (italics) to denote the value of a control at a certain time. Thus u denotes a mapping, whereas u denotes a point in $R ^ { k }$ 

Suppose now that we have chosen a fixed control law $\mathbf { u } ( t , \mathrm { x } )$ . Then we can insert u into (19.12) to obtain the standard SDE 

$$
\mathrm{d} X _ {t} = \mu (t, X _ {t}, \mathbf {u} (t, X _ {t})) \mathrm{d} t + \sigma (t, X _ {t}, \mathbf {u} (t, X _ {t})) \mathrm{d} W _ {t}.\tag{19.14}
$$

In most concrete cases we also have to satisfy some control constraints, and we model this by taking as given a fixed subset $U \subseteq R ^ { k }$ and requiring that $u _ { t } \in U$ for each t. We can now define the class of admissible control laws. 

Definition 19.1 A control law u is called admissible if 

${ \mathbf { u } } ( t , x ) \in U$ for all $t \in R _ { + }$ and all $\mathbf { X } \in \mathbf { R } ^ { \mathrm { n } }$ 

For any given initial point (t, x) the SDE 

$$
\mathrm{d} X _ {s} = \mu (s, X _ {s}, \mathbf {u} (s, X _ {s})) \mathrm{d} s + \sigma (s, X _ {s}, \mathbf {u} (s, X _ {s})) \mathrm{d} W _ {s},
$$

$$
X _ {t} = \mathrm{x}
$$

has a unique solution. 

I ;The class of admissible control laws is denoted by U. 

For a given control law u, the solution process X will of course depend on the initial value x, as well as on the chosen control law u. To be precise we should therefore denote the process X by $\pmb { X ^ { x , \mathbf { u } } }$ ", but sometimes we will suppress x or u. We note that eqn (19.14) looks rather messy, and since we will also have to deal with the It8 formula in connection with (19.14) we need some more streamlined notation. 

Definition 19.2 Consider eqn $( 1 9 . 1 4 )$ , and let ' denote matrix transpose. 

For any fied vector $\mathcal { U } \in R ^ { k }$ , the functions $\mu ^ { \mathfrak { u } } , \sigma ^ { \mathfrak { u } }$ , and $C ^ { \mathfrak { u } }$ are defined by 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \mu^ {u} (t, x) = \mu (t, x, u), \\ \sigma^ {u} (t, x) = \sigma (t, x, u), \\ C ^ {u} (t, x) = \sigma (t, x, u) \sigma (t, x, u) ^ {\prime}. \end{array}
$$

For any control law u, the functions $\mu ^ { \mathbf { u } } , \ a ^ { \upsilon } , \ C ^ { \upsilon } ( t , x )$ , and $\boldsymbol { F } ^ { U } ( t , \boldsymbol { x } )$ are defined by 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & {\mu^ {\mathbf {u}} (t, x) = \mu (t, x, \mathbf {u} (t, x)),} \\ & {\sigma^ {\mathbf {u}} (t, x) = \sigma (t, x, \mathbf {u} (t, x)),} \\ & {C ^ {\mathbf {u}} (t, x) = \sigma (t, x, \mathbf {u} (t, x)) \sigma (t, x, \mathbf {u} (t, x)) ^ {\prime},} \\ & {F ^ {U} (t, x) = F (t, x, \mathbf {u} (t, x)).} \end{array}
$$

For any fied vector $u \in R ^ { k }$ , the partial diffeerenticll operator $A ^ { \prime \prime }$ is defined by 

$$
\mathcal {A} ^ {u} = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} \mu_ {i} ^ {u} (t, x) \frac {\partial}{\partial x _ {i}} + \frac {1}{2} \sum_ {i, j = 1} ^ {n} C _ {i j} ^ {u} (t, x) \frac {\partial^ {2}}{\partial x _ {i} \partial x _ {j}}.
$$

For any control law u, the partial differential operator $d ^ { \prime \prime }$ is defined by 

$$
\mathcal {A} ^ {\mathbf {u}} = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} \mu_ {i} ^ {\mathbf {u}} (t, x) \frac {\partial}{\partial x _ {i}} + \frac {1}{2} \sum_ {i, j = 1} ^ {n} C _ {i j} ^ {\mathbf {u}} (t, x) \frac {\partial^ {2}}{\partial x _ {i} \partial x _ {j}}.
$$

Given a control law u we will sometimes write eqn (19.14) in a convenient shorthand notation as 

$$
\mathrm{d} X _ {t} ^ {\mathbf {u}} = \mu^ {\mathbf {u}} d t + \sigma^ {\mathbf {u}} \mathrm{d} W _ {t}.\tag{19.15}
$$

For a given control law u with a corresponding controlled process $X ^ { v }$ we will also often use the shorthand notation $\mathbf { u } _ { t }$ instead of the clumsier e: u $( t , X _ { t } ^ { \mathbf { u } } )$ 

The reader should be aware of the fact that the existence assumption in the definition above is not at all an innocent one. In many cases it is natural to consider control laws which are "rapidly varying", i.e. feedback laws $\mathbf { u } ( t , \mathbf { x } )$ which are very irregular as functions of the state variable x. Inserting such an 

irregular control law into the state dynamics will easily give us a very irregular drift function $\mu ( \mathfrak { t } , \mathfrak { x } , \mathfrak { u } ( t , \mathfrak { x } ) )$ (as a function of x), and we may find ourselves outside the nice Lipschitz situation in Proposition 5.1, thus leaving us with a I highly nontrivial existence problem. The reader is referred to the literature for details. 

We now go on to the objective function of the control problem, and therefore we consider as given a pair of functions 

$$
\begin{array}{l} {F: R _ {+} \times R ^ {n} \times R ^ {k} \to R,} \\ {\Phi : R ^ {n} \to R.} \end{array}
$$

Now we define the value function of our problem as the function 

$$
\mathcal {J} _ {0}: \mathcal {U} \to R,
$$

defined by 

$$
\mathcal {J} _ {0} (\mathbf {u}) = E \left[ \int_ {0} ^ {T} F (t, X _ {t} ^ {\mathbf {u}}, \mathbf {u} _ {t}) \mathrm{d} t + \Phi (X _ {T} ^ {\mathbf {u}}) \right],
$$

where $\mathbf { x } ^ { \mathrm { { u } } }$ is the solution to (19.14) with the given initial condition $X _ { 0 } = x _ { 0 }$ 

Our formal problem can thus be written as that of maximizing $\mathcal { I } _ { 0 } ( \mathbf { u } )$ over all ${ \mathrm {  ~ u ~ } } \in \mathcal { U } ,$ , and we define the optimal value <sub>by</sub> $\mathcal { \hat { I } } _ { 0 }$ 

$$
\hat {\mathcal {J}} _ {0} = \sup _ {\mathbf {u} \in \mathcal {U}} \mathcal {J} _ {0} (\mathrm{u}).
$$

If there exists an admissible control law u with the property that 

$$
\mathcal {I} _ {0} (\hat {\mathbf {u}}) = \hat {\mathcal {J}} _ {0},
$$

then we say that u is an optimal control law for the given problem. Note that, as for any optimization problem, the optimal law may not exist. For a given concrete control problem our main objective is of course to find the optimal control law (if it exists), or at least to learn something about the qualitative behavior of the optimal law. 

19.3 T h e Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman Equation 

Given an optimal control problem we have two natural questions to answer: 

(a) Does there exist an optimal control law? 

(b) Given that an optimal control exists, how do we find it? 

In this text we will mainly be concerned with problem (b) above, and the methodology used will be that of dynamic programming. The main idea is to embed our original problem into a much larger class of problems, and then to tie all these problems together with a PDE known as the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation. The control problem is then shown to be equivalent to the problem of finding a solution to the HJB equation. 

We will now describe the embedding procedure, and for that purpose we choose a fixed point t in time, with $0 \leq \mathfrak { t } \leq \mathrm { T }$ . We also choose a fixed point x in the state space, i.e. $\mathbf { X } \in \mathbf { R } ^ { \mathrm { n } }$ . For this fixed pair (t, x) we now define the following control problem. 

Definition 19.3 The control problem $\mathcal { P } ( t , { \pmb x } )$ is defined as the problem to maximize 

$$
E _ {t, x} \left[ \int_ {t} ^ {T} F (s, X _ {s} ^ {\mathbf {u}}, \mathbf {u} _ {s}) \mathrm{d} s + \Phi (X _ {T} ^ {\mathbf {u}}) \right],\tag{19.16}
$$

given the dynamics 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \mathrm{d} X _ {s} ^ {\mathbf {u}} = \mu (s, X _ {s} ^ {\mathbf {u}}, \mathbf {u} (s, X _ {s} ^ {\mathbf {u}})) \mathrm{d} s + \sigma (s, X _ {s} ^ {\mathbf {u}}, \mathbf {u} (s, X _ {s} ^ {\mathbf {u}})) \mathrm{d} W _ {s}, \\ X _ {t} = \mathrm{x}, \end{array}\tag{19.17}
$$

(19.18) 

and the constmints 

$$
\mathbf {u} (s, y) \in U, \quad \forall (s, y) \in [ t, T ] \times R ^ {n}.\tag{19.19}
$$

Observe that we use the notation s and y above because the letters t and x are already used to denote the fixed chosen point $( t , \pmb { x } )$ . 

We note that in terms of the definition above, our original problem is the problem ${ \mathcal { P } } ( 0 , x _ { 0 } )$ ) . A somewhat drastic interpretation of the problem $\mathcal { P } ( t , { \mathbf { x } } )$ is that you have fallen asleep at time zero. Suddenly you wake up, noticing that the time now is t and that your state process while you were asleep has moved to the point x. You now try to do as well as possible under the circumstances, so you want to maximize your utility over the remaining time, given the fact that you start at time t in the state x. 

We now define the value function and the optimal value function. 

Definition 19.4 

The value function 

$$
\mathcal {J}: R _ {+} \times R ^ {n} \times \mathcal {U} \rightarrow R
$$

is defined by 

$$
\mathcal {J} (t, x, \mathbf {u}) = E \left[ \int_ {t} ^ {T} F (s, X _ {s} ^ {\mathbf {u}}, \mathbf {u} _ {s}) d s + \Phi (X _ {T} ^ {\mathbf {u}}) \right]
$$

given the dynamzcs (19.17)-(19.18). 

The optimal value function 

$$
V: R _ {+} \times R ^ {n} \rightarrow R
$$

is defined by 

$$
V (t, \mathrm{x}) = \sup _ {\mathbf {u} \in \mathcal {U}} \mathcal {J} (t, \mathrm{x}, \mathrm{u}).
$$

Thus $\mathcal { I } ( t , \mathbf { x } , \mathbf { u } )$ is the expected utility of using the control law u over the time interval [t, TI, given the fact that you start in state x at time t. The optimal value function gives you the optimal expected utility over [t, TI under the same initial conditions. 

The main object of interest for us is the optimal value function, and we now go on to derive a PDE for V. It should be noted that this derivation is largely heuristic. We make some rather strong regularity assumptions, and we disregard a number of technical problems. We will comment on these problems later, but to see exactly which problems we are ignoring we now make some basic assumptions. 

## Assumption 19.3.1 We assume the following:

1. There exists an optimal control law u. 

2. The optimal value function V is regular in the sense that $\mathrm { V } \in C ^ { 1 , 2 }$ 

3. A number of limiting procedures in the following arguments can be justified. 

We now go on to derive the PDE, and to this end we fix $( \mathbf { t } , \mathbf { x } ) \in ( 0 , \mathrm { T } ) \mathrm { ~ x ~ } R ^ { n }$ Furthermore we choose a real number h (interpreted as a "small" time increment) <sub>such</sub> <sub>that</sub> <sub>t</sub> + h < <sub>T.</sub> <sub>We</sub> <sub>choose</sub> <sub>a</sub> <sub>fixed</sub> <sub>but</sub> <sub>arbitrary</sub> <sub>control</sub> <sub>law</sub> <sub>u,</sub> <sub>and</sub> <sub>define</sub> the control law $\mathtt { u } ^ { * }$ by 

$$
\mathbf {u} ^ {\star} (s, y) = \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} \mathbf {u} (s, y), & (s, y) \in [ t, t + h ] \times R ^ {n}, \\ \hat {\mathbf {u}} (s, y), & (s, y) \in (t + h, T ] \times R ^ {n}. \end{array} \right.
$$

In other words, if we use $\mathtt { u } ^ { * }$ then we use the arbitrary control u during the time interval $[ \mathfrak { t } , \mathfrak { t } + \mathfrak { h } ]$ , and then we switch to the optimal control law during the rest of the time period. 

The whole idea of dynamic programming actually boils down to the following procedure: 

First, given the point $( t , x )$ as above, we consider the following two strategies over the time interval $[ \mathbf { t } , T ]$ : 

S t r a t e g y I. Use the optimal law Ez. 

Strategy 11. Use the control law u* defined above. 

We then compute the expected utilities obtained by the respective strategies. 

Finally, using the obvious fact that Strategy I by definition has to be at least as good as Strategy 11, and letting h tend to zero, we obtain our fundamental PDE. 

We now carry out this program. 

Expected utility for strategy I: This is trivial, since by definition the utility is the optimal one given by $\mathcal { I } ( t , x , \mathrm { u } ) = V ( t , \mathrm { x } )$ 

Expected utility for strategy 11: We divide the time interval $[ t , T ]$ into two parts, the intervals $[ \mathfrak { t } , \mathfrak { t } + \mathfrak { h } ]$ and $( \mathrm { t } + \mathrm { h } , T ]$ I, respectively. 

The expected utility, using Strategy 11, for the interval $\left[ \operatorname { t } , \operatorname { t } + \operatorname { h } \right)$ is given by 

$$
E _ {t, x} \left[ \int_ {t} ^ {t + h} F (\mathbf {s}, X _ {s} ^ {\mathbf {u}}, \mathbf {u} _ {s}) \mathrm{ds} \right].
$$

In the interval $[ \mathrm { t } + h , T ]$ we observe that at time $\mathrm { ~ t ~ } { + }$ h we will be in the (stochastic) state $X _ { t + h } ^ { u }$ h.. Since, by definition, we will use the optimal strategy during the entire interval $[ \mathrm { t } + h , T ]$ we see that the remaining expected utility at time t + h is given by $\mathrm { V } ( \mathrm { t } { \ + } \mathrm { h } , X _ { t + h } ^ { \mathbf { u } } )$ ). Thus the expected utility over the interval $[ \mathbf { t } + \mathbf { h } , T ]$ , conditional on the fact that at time t we are in state x, is given by 

$$
E _ {t, x} \left[ V (t + h, X _ {t + h} ^ {\mathbf {u}}) \right].
$$

Thus the total expected utility for Strategy I1 is 

$$
E _ {t, x} \left[ \int_ {t} ^ {t + h} F (s, X _ {s} ^ {\mathbf {u}}, \mathbf {u} _ {s}) \mathrm{ds} + V (t + h, X _ {t + h} ^ {\mathbf {u}}) \right].
$$

Comparing the strategies: We now go on to compare the two strategies, and since by definition Strategy I is the optimal one, we must have the inequality 

$$
V (t, x) \geq E _ {t, x} \left[ \int_ {t} ^ {\mathrm{t+h}} F \left(s, X _ {s} ^ {\mathbf {u}}, \mathbf {u} _ {s}\right) \mathrm{d} s + V (t + h, X _ {t + h} ^ {\mathbf {u}}) \right]\tag{19.20}
$$

We also note that the inequality sign is due to the fact that the arbitrarily chosen control law u which we use on the interval $[ \mathrm { t } , \mathrm { t } + \mathrm { h } ]$ need not be the optimal one. In particular we have the following obvious fact. 

Remark 19.3.1 We have equality in (19.20) if and only if the control law u is an optimal law u. (Note that the optimal law does not have to be unique.) 

Since, by assumption, V is smooth we now use the It6 formula to obtain (with obvious notation) 

$$
\begin{array}{l} V (t + \mathrm{h}, X _ {t + h} ^ {\mathbf {u}}) = V (t, \mathrm{x}) + \int_ {t} ^ {t + h} \left\{\frac {\partial V}{\partial t} (s, X _ {s} ^ {\mathbf {u}}) + \mathcal {A} ^ {\mathbf {u}} V (s, X _ {s} ^ {\mathbf {u}}) \right\} \mathrm{d} s \\ + \int_ {t} ^ {t + h} \nabla_ {x} V (s, X _ {s} ^ {\mathbf {u}}) \sigma^ {\mathbf {u}} \mathrm{d} W _ {s}. \end{array}\tag{19.21}
$$

If we apply the expectation operator $\boldsymbol { E } _ { t , x }$ to this equation, and assume enough integrability, then the stochastic integral will vanish. We can then insert the resulting equation into the inequality (19.20). The term $V ( t , { \bf x } )$ will cancel, leaving us with the inequality 

$$
E _ {t, x} \left[ \int_ {t} ^ {t + h} \left[ F (s, X _ {s} ^ {\mathbf {u}}, \mathbf {u} _ {s}) + \frac {\partial \mathrm{Y}}{\partial t} (s, X _ {s} ^ {\mathbf {u}}) + \mathcal {A} ^ {\mathbf {u}} V (s, X _ {s} ^ {\mathbf {u}}) \right] \mathrm{d} s \right] \leq 0.\tag{19.22}
$$

Going to t h e limit: Now we divide by h, move h within the expectation and let h tend to zero. Assuming enough regularity to allow us to take the limit within the expectation, using the fundamental theorem of integral calculus, and recalling that $X _ { t } = \mathrm { x }$ , we get 

$$
F (t, x, u) + \frac {\partial V}{\partial t} (t, x) + \mathcal {A} ^ {u} V (t, x) \leq 0,\tag{19.23}
$$

where u denotes the value of the law u evaluated at (t, x), i.e. $\mathbf { u } = \mathbf { u } ( t , \mathbf { x } )$ . Since the control law u was arbitrary, this inequality will hold for all choices of ${ \mathbf { u } } \in U ,$ and we will have equality if and only if $\mathbf { u } = \hat { \mathbf { u } } ( t , \mathbf { x } )$ . We thus have the following equation: 

$$
\frac {\partial V}{\partial t} (t, \mathrm{x}) + \sup _ {u \in U} \{F (t, x, u) + \mathrm{duV(t,x)}) = 0.
$$

During the discussion the point (t, x) was fixed, but since it was chosen as an arbitrary point we see that the equation holds in fact for all $( \mathbf { t } , \mathbf { x } ) \in ( 0 , \mathbf { T } ) \mathrm { ~ x ~ } \pmb { R } ^ { n }$ Thus we have a (nonstandard type of) PDE, and we obviously need some boundary conditions. One such condition is easily obtained, since we obviously (why?) have $V ( T , x ) = \Phi ( x )$ ) for all $\mathbf { X } \in \pmb { R } ^ { n }$ . We have now arrived at our goal, amilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation, (often referred to as the HJB equation.) 

Theorem 19.5 (Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation) Under Assumption 19.3.1, the following hold: 

1. V satisfies the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation 

$$
\left\{ \begin{array}{c} \frac {\partial V}{\partial t} (t, x) + \sup _ {u \in U} \left\{F (t, x, u) + \mathcal {A} ^ {u} V (t, x) \right\} = 0, \quad \forall (t, x) \in (0, T) \times R ^ {n} \\ V (T, x) = \Phi (x), \quad \forall x \in R ^ {n}. \end{array} \right.
$$

2. For each $( \mathrm { t } , \mathrm { x } ) \in [ 0 , T ] \mathrm { ~ x ~ } \pmb { R ^ { n } }$ the supremum in the HJB equation above is attained by $\mathbf { u } = \hat { \mathbf { u } } ( t , \mathbf { x } )$ 

Remark 19.3.2 By going through the arguments above, it is easily seen that we may allow the constraint set $\dot { U }$ to be time- and state-dependent. If we thus have control constraints of the form 

$$
u (t, x) \in U (t, x), \quad \forall t, x
$$

then the HJB equation still holds with the obvious modification of the supremum part. 

It is important to note that this theorem has the form of a necessary condition. It says that if V is the optimal value function, and if ii is the optimal control, then V satisfies the HJB equation, and $\hat { \bf u } ( t , x )$ realizes the supremum in the equation. We also note that Assumption 19.3.1 is an ad hoc assumption. One would prefer to have conditions in terms of the initial data $\mu , \bar { \mathbf { \Omega } } , \mathbf { F } ,$ , and $\Phi$ which would guarantee that Assumption 19.3.1 is satisfied. This can in fact be done, but at a fairly high price in terms of technical complexity. The reader is referred to the specialist literature. 

A gratifying, and perhaps surprising, fact is that the HJB equation also acts as a sufficient condition for the optimal control problem. This result is known as the verification theorem for dynamic programming, and we will use it repeatedly below. Note that, as opposed to the necessary conditions above, the verification theorem is very easy to prove rigorously. 

Theorem 19.6 (Verification theorem) Suppose that we have two functions $H ( t , { \dot { x } } )$ and ${ \pmb g } ( t , { \bf x } )$ , such that 

a H is suficiently integrable (see Remark 19.3.4 below), and solves the HJB equation 

$$
\left\{ \begin{array}{c} \frac {\partial H}{\partial t} (t, x) + \sup _ {u \in U} \left\{F (t, x, u) + \mathcal {A} ^ {u} H (t, x) \right\} = 0, \quad \forall (t, x) \in (0, T) \times R ^ {n} \\ H (T, x) = \Phi (x), \quad \forall x \in \mathrm{R} ^ {n}. \end{array} \right.
$$

The function g is an admissible control law. 

a For each jixed (t, x), the supremum in the expression 

$$
\sup _ {u \in U} \{F (t, x, \mathrm{u}) + \mathcal {A} ^ {u} H (t, x) \}
$$

is attained by the choice $u = g ( t , \mathbf { x } )$ 

Then the following hold: 

1. The optimal value function V to the control problem is given by 

$$
V (t, \mathrm{x}) = H (t, x).
$$

2. There exists an optimal control law u, and in fact $\hat { \mathbf { u } } ( t , \mathrm { x } ) = g ( t , x )$ 

Remark 19.3.3 Note that we have used the letter H (instead of V) in the HJB equation above. This is because the letter V by definition denotes the optimal value function. 

Proof Assume that H and g axe given as above. Now choose an arbitrary control law $\mathbf { u } \in \mathcal { U }$ , and fix a point $\displaystyle ( \mathbf { t } , \mathbf { x } )$ . We define the process $\mathbf { X } ^ { \mathbf { u } }$ on the time interval [t, T] as the solution to the equation 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & {\mathrm{d} X _ {s} ^ {\mathbf {u}} = \mu^ {\mathbf {u}} (\mathrm{s}, X _ {s} ^ {\mathbf {u}}) \mathrm{ds} + \sigma^ {\mathbf {u}} (\mathrm{s}, X _ {s} ^ {\mathbf {u}}) \mathrm{d} W _ {s},} \\ & {\quad X _ {t} = \mathrm{x}.} \end{array}
$$

Inserting the process $X ^ { \mathrm { { U } } }$ into the function H and using the It6 formula we obtain 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & H (T, X _ {T} ^ {\mathbf {u}}) = H (t, x) + \int_ {t} ^ {T} \left\{\frac {\partial H}{\partial t} (s, X _ {s} ^ {\mathbf {u}}) + (\mathcal {A} ^ {\mathbf {u}} H) (s, X _ {s} ^ {\mathbf {u}}) \right\} \mathrm{d} s \\ & \qquad + \int_ {t} ^ {T} \nabla_ {x} H (s, X _ {s} ^ {\mathbf {u}}) \sigma^ {\mathbf {u}} (s, X _ {s} ^ {\mathbf {u}}) \mathrm{d} W _ {s}. \end{array}
$$

Since H solves the HJB equation we see that 

$$
\frac {\partial H}{\partial t} (t, x) + F (t, x, u) + \mathcal {A} ^ {u} H (t, x) \leq 0
$$

for all $u \in U$ , and thus we have, for each s and P-a.s, the inequality 

$$
\frac {\partial H}{\partial t} (s, X _ {s} ^ {\mathbf {u}}) + (\mathcal {A} ^ {\mathbf {u}} H) (\mathrm{a}, X _ {s} ^ {\mathbf {u}}) \leq - F ^ {\mathbf {u}} (s, X _ {s} ^ {\mathbf {u}}).
$$

From the boundary condition for the HJB equation we also have $H ( T , X _ { T } ^ { \mathbf { u } } ) =$ $\Phi ( X _ { T } ^ { \mathbf { u } } )$ ?), so we obtain the inequality 

$$
H (t, x) \geq \int_ {t} ^ {T} F ^ {\mathbf {u}} (s, X _ {s} ^ {\mathbf {u}}) \mathrm{d} s + \Phi (X _ {T} ^ {\mathbf {u}}) - \int_ {t} ^ {T} \nabla_ {x} H (s, X _ {s} ^ {\mathbf {u}}) \sigma^ {\mathbf {u}} \mathrm{d} W _ {s}.
$$

Taking expectations, and assuming enough integrability, we make the stochastic integral vanish, leaving us with the inequality 

$$
H (t, \mathbf {x}) \geq E _ {t, x} \left[ \int_ {t} ^ {T} F ^ {\mathbf {u}} (s, X _ {s} ^ {\mathbf {u}}) \mathrm{d} s + \Phi (X _ {T} ^ {\mathbf {u}}) \right] = \mathcal {J} (t, x, \mathbf {u}).
$$

Since the control law u was arbitrarily chosen this gives us 

$$
H (t, \mathrm{x}) \geq \sup _ {\mathbf {u} \in \mathcal {U}} \mathcal {J} (t, \mathrm{x}, \mathrm{u}) = V (t, x).\tag{19.24}
$$

To obtain the reverse inequality we choose the specific control law $\mathbf { u } ( t , \mathbf { x } ) =$ ${ \pmb g } ( { \pmb t } , { \pmb x } )$ . Going through the same calculations as above, and using the fact that by assumption we have 

$$
\frac {\partial H}{\partial t} (t, x) + \mathrm{F} ^ {\mathrm{g}} (\mathrm{t,x}) + \mathrm{d} ^ {\mathrm{g}} \mathrm{H(t,x)} = 0,
$$

we obtain the equality 

$$
\boldsymbol {H} (t, \boldsymbol {x}) = E _ {t, \boldsymbol {x}} \left[ \int_ {t} ^ {T} F ^ {\mathbf {g}} (s, X _ {s} ^ {\mathbf {g}}) \mathrm{d} s + \Phi (X _ {T} ^ {\mathbf {g}}) \right] = \mathcal {J} (t, x, \mathbf {g}).\tag{19.25}
$$

On the other hand we have the trivial inequality 

$$
V (t, \boldsymbol {x}) \geq \mathcal {J} (t, \boldsymbol {x}, \mathbf {g}),\tag{19.26}
$$

so, using (19.24)-(19.26), we obtain 

$$
\boldsymbol {H} (t, \boldsymbol {x}) \geq V (t, \boldsymbol {x}) \geq \mathcal {J} (t, x, \mathrm{g}) = H (t, x).
$$

This shows that in fact 

$$
\boldsymbol {H} (\boldsymbol {t}, \boldsymbol {x}) = \boldsymbol {V} (\boldsymbol {t}, \boldsymbol {x}) = \mathcal {J} (t, \boldsymbol {x}, \mathbf {g}),
$$

which proves that H = V, and that gs is the optimal control law. 

Remark 19.3.4 The assumption that H is "sufficiently integrable" in the theorem above is made in order for the stochastic integral in the proof to have expected value zero. This will be the case if, for example, H satisifes the condition 

$$
\nabla_ {\boldsymbol {x}} H (\boldsymbol {s}, X _ {s} ^ {\mathbf {u}}) \sigma^ {\mathbf {u}} (s, X _ {s} ^ {\mathbf {u}}) \in £ ^ {2},
$$

for all admissible control laws. 

Remark 19.3.5 Sometimes, instead of a maximization problem, we consider a minimization problem. Of course we now make the obvious definitions for the value function and the optimal value function. It is then easily seen that all the results above still hold if the expression 

$$
\sup _ {\boldsymbol {u} \in U} \left\{\boldsymbol {F} (\boldsymbol {t}, \boldsymbol {x}, \mathrm{u}) + \mathrm{d} ^ {\mathrm{U}} \mathrm{V} (\mathrm{t}, \mathrm{x})\right)
$$

in the HJB equation is replaced by the expression 

$$
\inf _ {\boldsymbol {u} \in U} \left\{\boldsymbol {F} (\boldsymbol {t}, \boldsymbol {x}, \mathrm{u}) + \mathrm{A} ^ {\mathrm{U}} \mathrm{V} (\mathrm{t}, \mathrm{x})\right).
$$

Remark 19.3.6 In the Verification Theorem we may allow the control constraint set U to be state and time dependent, i.e. of the form $U ( \mathbf { t } , \mathbf { x } )$ 

## 19.4 Handling the HJB Equation

In this section we will describe the actual handling of the HJB equation, and in the next section we will study a classical example-the linear quadratic regulator. We thus consider our standard optimal control problem with the corresponding HJB equation: 

$$
\left\{ \begin{array}{c} \frac {\partial V}{\partial t} (t, \mathrm{x}) + \sup _ {u \in U} \{F (t, x, u) + \mathrm{duV(t,x)} \} = 0, \\ V (T, \mathrm{x}) = \Phi (x). \end{array} \right.\tag{19.27}
$$

Schematically, we now proceed as follows: 

1. Consider the HJB equation as a PDE for an unknown function V. 

2. Fix an arbitrary point $( \mathrm { t } , \mathrm { x } ) \in [ 0 , T ] \times \mathrm { R } ^ { \mathrm { n } }$ and solve, for this fixed choice of (t, x) , the static optimization problem 

$$
\max _ {\boldsymbol {u} \in U} [ F (\boldsymbol {t}, \mathrm{x}, \mathrm{u}) + \mathrm{AuV} (\mathrm{t}, \boldsymbol {x}) ]
$$

Note that in this problem u is the only variable, whereas t and x are considered to be fixed parameters. The functions F, p, u, and V are considered as given. 

3. The optimal choice of u, denoted by $\hat { u } ,$ will of course depend on our choice of t and x, but it will also depend on the function V and its various partial derivatives (which are hiding under the sign duV). To highlight these dependencies we write ii as 

$$
\hat {\mathbf {u}} = \hat {\mathbf {u}} (t, x; V).\tag{19.28}
$$

4. The function $4 \left( { \bf t , x ; V } \right)$ is our candidate for the optimal control law, but since we do not know V this description is incomplete. Therefore we substitute the expression for 4 in (19.28) into the PDE (19.27), giving us the PDE 

$$
\frac {\mathrm{d} V}{\widehat {\pmb {x}}} (t, \mathrm{x}) + F ^ {\hat {\mathbf {u}}} (t, \mathrm{x}) + \mathcal {A} ^ {\hat {\mathbf {u}}} V (t, \pmb {x}) = 0,\tag{19.29}
$$

$$
V (T, \boldsymbol {x}) = \Phi (\boldsymbol {x}).\tag{19.30}
$$

5. Now we solve the PDE above! (See the remark below.) Then we put the solution V into expression (19.28). Using the verification theorem 19.6 we can now identify V as the optimal value function, and 4 as the optimal control law. 

Remark 19.4.1 The hard work of dynamic programming consists in solving the highly nonlinear PDE in step 5 above. There are of course no general analytic methods available for this, so the number of known optimal control problems with an analytic solution is very small indeed. In an actual case one usually tries to guess a solution, i.e. we typically make an ansatz for V, parameterized by a finite number of parameters, and then we use the PDE in order to identify the parameters. The making of an ansatz is often helped by the intuitive observation that if there is an analytical solution to the problem, then it seems likely that V inherits some structural properties from the boundary function as well as from the instantaneous utility function F. 

For a general problem there is thus very little hope of obtaining an analytic solution, and it is worth pointing out that many of the known solved control problems have, to some extent, been "rigged" in order to be analytically solvable. 

## 19.5 The Linear Regulator

We now want to put the ideas from the previous section into action, and for this purpose we study the most well known of all control problems, namely the linear quadratic regulator problem. In this classical engineering example we wish to minimize 

$$
E \left[ \int_ {0} ^ {T} \left\{X _ {t} ^ {\prime} Q X _ {t} + u _ {t} ^ {\prime} R u _ {t} \right\} \mathrm{d} t + X _ {T} ^ {\prime} H X _ {T} \right],
$$

(where I denotes transpose) given the dynamics 

$$
\mathrm{d} X _ {t} = \left\{A X _ {t} + B u _ {t} \right\} \mathrm{d} t + C \mathrm{d} W _ {t}.
$$

One interpretation of this problem is that we want to control a vehicle in such a way that it stays close to the origin (the terms $x ^ { \prime } Q x$ and ${ \pmb x } ^ { \prime } H { \pmb x } )$ while at the same time keeping the "energy" utRu small. 

As usual $X _ { t } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { \mathrm { n } }$ and $\mathbf { u } _ { t } \in R ^ { k }$ ~ , and we impose no control constraints on u. The matrices Q, R, H , A, B, and C are assumed to be known. Without loss of generality we may assume that Q, R, and H are symmetric, and we assume that R is positive definite (and thus invertible). 

The HJB equation now becomes 

$$
\left\{ \begin{array}{l} \frac {\partial V}{\partial t} (t, x) + \inf _ {u \in R ^ {k}} \left\{x ^ {t} Q x + u ^ {\prime} R u + [ \nabla_ {x} V ] (t, x) [ A x + B u ] \right\} \\ \quad + \frac {1}{2} \sum_ {i, j} \frac {\partial^ {2} V}{\partial x _ {i} \partial x _ {j}} (t, x) [ C C ^ {\prime} ] _ {i, j} = 0, \\ V (T, x) = x ^ {\prime} H x. \end{array} \right.
$$

For each fixed choice of $^ { ( t , \mathrm { x } ) }$ we now have to solve the static unconstrained optimization problem to minimize 

$$
u ^ {\prime} R u + [ \nabla_ {x} V ] (t, x) [ A x + B u ].
$$

Since, by assumption, $\mathbf R > 0$ we get the solution by setting the gradient equal to zero, thus giving us the equation 

$$
2 u ^ {\prime} R = - (\nabla_ {x} V) B,
$$

which gives us the optimal u as 

$$
\hat {u} = - \frac {1}{2} R ^ {- 1} B ^ {\prime} (\nabla_ {x} V) ^ {\prime}.
$$

Here we see clearly (compare point 2 in the scheme above) that in order to use this formula we need to know V, and we thus try to make an educated guess about the structure of V. From the boundary value function $\pmb { x } ^ { \prime } \pmb { H } \pmb { x }$ and the quadratic term $x ^ { \prime } Q x$ in the instantaneous cost function it seems reasonable to assume that V is a quadratic function. Consequently we make the following ansatz: 

$$
V (t, x) = x ^ {\prime} P (t) x + q (t),
$$

where we assume that $P ( t )$ is a deterministic symmetric matrix function of time, whereas $q ( t )$ ) is a scalar deterministic function. It would of course also be natural to include a linear term of the form $L ( t ) x$ , but it turns out that this is not necessary. 

With this trial solution we have, suppressing the t-variable and denoting time derivatives by a dot, 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \frac {\partial V}{\partial t} (t, x) = x ^ {\prime} \dot {P} x + \dot {q}, \\ \nabla_ {x} V (t, x) = 2 x ^ {\prime} P, \\ \nabla_ {x x} V (t, x) = 2 P \\ \hat {u} = - R ^ {- 1} B ^ {\prime} P x. \end{array}
$$

Inserting these expressions into the HJB equation we get 

$$
\begin{array}{l} x ^ {\prime} \dot {P} x + \dot {q} + x ^ {\prime} Q x + x ^ {\prime} P B R ^ {- 1} R R ^ {- 1} B ^ {\prime} P x + 2 x ^ {\prime} P A x \\ - 2 x ^ {\prime} P B R ^ {- 1} B ^ {\prime} P x + \sum_ {i, j} P _ {i j} [ C C ^ {\prime} ] _ {i j} = 0. \end{array}
$$

We note that the last term above equals $\operatorname { t r } [ \mathbf { C } ^ { \mathrm { { t } } } \mathbf { P } \mathbf { C } ]$ , where tr denote the trace of a matrix, and furthermore we see that $2 x ^ { \prime } P A x = x ^ { \prime } A ^ { \prime } P x + x ^ { \prime } P A x$ (this is just cosmetic). Collecting terms gives us 

$$
x ^ {\prime} \left\{\dot {P} + Q - P B R ^ {- 1} B ^ {\prime} P + A ^ {\prime} P + P A \right\} x + \dot {q} + \operatorname{tr} [ C ^ {\prime} P C ] = 0.\tag{19.31}
$$

If this equation is to hold for all x and all t then firstly the bracket must vanish, leaving us with the matrix ODE 

$$
\mathrm{P} = P B R ^ {- 1} B ^ {\prime} P - \mathrm {A^ {\prime} P- PA - Q}.
$$

We are then left with the scalar equation 

$$
\dot {q} = - \operatorname{tr} [ C ^ {\prime} P C ].
$$

We now need some boundary values for P and ${ \mathfrak { q } } ,$ but these follow immediately from the boundary conditions of the HJB equation. We thus end up with the foll~wing pairs of equations: 

$$
\left\{ \begin{array}{l} P = P B R ^ {- 1} B ^ {\prime} P - A ^ {\prime} P - P A - Q, \\ P (T) = H. \\ \left\{ \begin{array}{c} \dot {q} = - \operatorname{tr} [ C ^ {\prime} P C ], \\ q (T) = 0. \end{array} \right. \end{array} \right.\tag{19.32}
$$

(19.33) 

The matrix equation (19.32) is known as a Riccati equation, and there are powerful algorithms available for solving it numerically. The equation for q can then be integrated directly. 

Summing up we see that the optimal value function and the optimal control law are given by the following formulas. Note that the optimal control is linear in the state variable. 

$$
V (t, x) = x ^ {\prime} P (t) x + \int_ {t} ^ {T} \operatorname{tr} [ C ^ {\prime} P (s) C ] \mathrm{d} s,\tag{19.34}
$$

$$
\hat {\mathbf {u}} (t, x) = - R ^ {- 1} B ^ {\prime} P (t) x.\tag{19.35}
$$

## 19.6 Optimal Consumption and Investment

## 19.6.1 A Generalization

In many concrete applications, in particular in economics, it is natural to consider an optimal control problem, where the state variable is constrained to stay within a prespecified domain. As an example it may be reasonable to demand that the wealth of an investor is never allowed to become negative. We will now generalize our class of optimal control problems to allow for such considerations. 

Let us therefore consider the following controlled SDE: 

$$
\mathrm{d} X _ {t} = \mu (t, X _ {t}, u _ {t}) \mathrm{d} t + \sigma (t, X _ {t}, u _ {t}) \mathrm{d} W _ {t},\tag{19.36}
$$

$$
X _ {0} = x _ {0},\tag{19.37}
$$

where as before we impose the control constraint $u _ { t } \in U$ . We also consider as given a fixed time interval [0, TI, and a fixed domain $\mathbf { D } \subseteq [ 0 , T ] \mathrm { ~ x ~ } \mathbf { R ^ { n } }$ , and the basic idea is that when the state process hits the boundary dD of D, then the activity is at an end. It is thus natural to define the stopping time T by 

$$
\tau = \inf \left\{t \geq 0 | (t, X _ {t}) \in \partial D \right\} \mathrm{AT},
$$

where x $\mathrm { \ A \ y } = \mathrm { \mathbf { m i n } } [ { \pmb x } , { \bf y } ]$ . We consider as given an instantaneous utility function $F ( t , x , u )$ and a "bequest function" $\Phi ( t , \mathbf { x } )$ , i.e. a mapping ${ \bar { \Phi } } : \partial D \to R$ . The control problem to be considered is that of maximizing 

$$
E \left[ \int_ {0} ^ {\tau} F (s, X _ {s} ^ {\mathbf {u}}, \mathbf {u} _ {s}) \mathrm{d} s + \Phi (\tau , X _ {\tau} ^ {\mathbf {u}}) \right]\tag{19.38}
$$

In order for this problem to be interesting we have to demand that $X _ { 0 } \in D$ , and the interpretation is that when we hit the boundary $\partial D ,$ , the game is over and we obtain the bequest $\Phi \left( \tau , X _ { \tau } \right)$ ) . We see immediately that our earlier situation corresponds to the case when $\dot { D } = [ 0 , T ] \ x \ \mathrm { R } ^ { \mathrm { n } }$ and when $\Phi$ is constant in the t-variable. 

In order to analyze our present problem we may proceed as in the previous sections, introducing the value function and the optimal value function exactly as before. The only new technical problem encountered is that of considering a stochastic integral with a stochastic limit of integration. Since this will take us outside the scope of the present text we will confine ourselves to giving the results. The proofs are (modulo the technicalities mentioned above) exactly as before. 

## Theorem 19.7 (HJB equation) Assume that

The optimal value function V is in $C ^ { 1 , 2 }$ 

An optimal law u exists. 

Then the following hold: 

1. V satisifies the HJB equation 

$$
\left\{ \begin{array}{l} \frac {\partial V}{\partial t} (t, x) + \underset {u \in U} {\sup} \{F (t, x, u) + \mathcal {A} ^ {u} V (t, x) \} = 0, \quad \forall (t, x) \in D, \\ V (t, _ {X}) = \Phi (t, x), \quad \forall (t, _ {X}) \in \partial D. \end{array} \right.
$$

2. For each $( { \pmb t } , { \pmb x } ) \in D$ the supremum in the HJB equation above is attained by $\pmb { u } = \hat { \mathbf { u } } ( t , \pmb { x } )$ 

Theorem 19.8 (Verification theorem) Suppose that we have two functions $H ( t , x )$ and ${ \mathbf { } } g ( t , x )$ , such that 

H is suficiently integrable, and solves the HJB equation 

$$
\left\{ \begin{array}{l} \frac {\partial H}{\partial t} (t, x) + \sup _ {u \in U} \left\{F (t, x, u) + \mathcal {A} ^ {u} H (t, x) \right\} = 0, \quad \forall (t, x) \in D, \\ \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \bar {H} (t, x) \equiv \Phi (t, x), \quad \forall (t, x) \in \partial D. \end{array} \right.
$$

The function g is an admissible control law. 

For each jixed (t, x), the supremum in the expression 

$$
\sup _ {\boldsymbol {u} \in U} \left\{\boldsymbol {F} (t, \boldsymbol {x}, \mathrm{u}) + \mathrm{duH(t,x)} \right\}
$$

is attained by the choice $u = g ( t , \boldsymbol { x } )$ 

Then the following hold: 

1. The optimal value function V to the control problem is given by 

$$
V (t, x) = H (t, x).
$$

2. There exists an optimal control law ii, and in fact $\hat { \mathbf { u } } ( t , \mathbf { x } ) = g ( t , x )$ 

## 19.6.2 Optimal Consumption

In order to illustrate the technique we will now go back to the optimal consump tion problem at the beginning of the chapter. We thus consider the problem of maximizing 

$$
E \left[ \int_ {0} ^ {T} F (t, c _ {t}) \mathrm{d} t + \Phi (X _ {T}) \right],\tag{19.39}
$$

given the wealth dynamics 

$$
\mathrm{d} X _ {t} = X _ {t} \left[ u _ {t} ^ {0} r + u _ {t} ^ {1} \alpha \right] \mathrm{d} t - c _ {t} \mathrm{d} t + u ^ {1} \sigma X _ {t} \mathrm{d} W _ {t}.\tag{19.40}
$$

As usual we impose the control constraints 

$$
\begin{array}{r} c _ {t} \geq 0, \quad \forall t \geq 0, \\ u _ {t} ^ {0} + u _ {t} ^ {1} = 1, \quad \forall t \geq 0. \end{array}
$$

In a control problem of this kind it is important to be aware of the fact that one may quite easily formulate a nonsensical problem. To take a simple example, suppose that we have $\Phi = 0$ , and suppose that F is increasing and unbounded in the c-variable. Then the problem above degenerates completely. It does not possess an optimal solution at all, and the reason is of course that the consumer can increase his/her utility to any given level by simply consuming an arbitrarily large amount at every t. The consequence of this hedonistic behavior is of course the fact that the wealth process will, with very high probability, become negative, but this is neither prohibited by the control constraints, nor punished by any bequest function. 

An elegant way out of this dilemma is to choose the domain D of the preceding section as $\mathrm { D } = [ 0 , T ] \times \{ x | x > 0 )$ . With T defined as above this means, in concrete terms, that 

$$
\tau = \inf \left\{t > 0 \mid X _ {t} = 0 \right\} \wedge T.
$$

A natural objective function in this case is thus given by 

$$
E \left[ \int_ {0} ^ {\tau} F (t, c _ {t}) \mathrm{d} t \right],\tag{19.41}
$$

which automatically ensures that when the consumer has no wealth, then al activity is terminated. 

We will now analyze this problem in some detail. Firstly we notice that we can get rid of the constraint $\dot { u _ { t } ^ { 0 } } + u _ { t } ^ { 1 } = 1$ by defining a new control variable w as $\mathrm { w } = u ^ { 1 }$ , and then substituting 1 - w for $u ^ { \flat }$ O. This gives us the state dynamics 

$$
\mathrm{d} X _ {t} = w _ {t} [ \mathrm{or} - \mathrm{r} ] X _ {t} \mathrm{d} t + (r X _ {t} - c _ {t}) \mathrm{d} t + w \sigma X _ {t} \mathrm{d} W _ {t},\tag{19.42}
$$

and the corresponding HJB equation is 

$$
\left\{ \begin{array}{l l} \frac {\partial V}{\partial t} + \sup _ {c \geq 0, w \in R} \bigg \{F (t, c) + w x (\alpha - r) \frac {\partial V}{\partial x} + (r x - c) \frac {\partial V}{\partial x} + \frac {1}{2} x ^ {2} w ^ {2} \sigma^ {2} \frac {\partial^ {2} V}{\partial x ^ {2}} \bigg \} = 0, \\ & V (T, x) = 0, \\ & V (t, 0) = 0. \end{array} \right.
$$

We now specialize our example to the case when F is of the form 

$$
F (t, c) = \mathrm{e} ^ {- \delta t} c ^ {\gamma},
$$

where $0 < \gamma < 1$ . The economic reasoning behind this is that we now have an infinite marginal utility a t ${ \mathrm { c } } = 0$ . This will force the optimal consumption plan to be positive throughout the planning period, a fact which will facilitate the analytical treatment of the problem. In terms of Remark 19.4.1 we are thu "rigging" the problem. 

The static optimization problem to be solved w.r.t. c and w is thus that of maximizing 

$$
\mathrm{e} ^ {- \delta t} c ^ {\gamma} + w x (\alpha - r) \frac {\mathrm{aV}}{\partial x} + (\mathrm{rX} - c) \frac {\mathrm{aV}}{\partial x} + \frac {1}{2} x ^ {2} \mathrm{w} ^ {2} \sigma^ {2} \frac {\partial^ {2} V}{\mathrm{aX} ^ {2}},
$$

and, assuming an interior solution, the first-order conditions are 

$$
\gamma c ^ {\gamma - 1} = \mathrm{e} ^ {\delta t} V _ {x},\tag{19.43}
$$

$$
w = \frac {- V _ {x}}{x \cdot V _ {x x}} \frac {\mathrm{a} - \mathrm{r}}{\sigma^ {2}},\tag{19.44}
$$

where we have used subscripts to denote partial derivatives. 

We again see that in order to implement the optimal consumption-investmen plan (19.43)-(19.44) we need to know the optimal value function V. We therefore suggest a trial solution (see Remark 19.4.1), and in view of the shape of the instantaneous utility function it is natural to try a V-function of the form 

$$
V (t, x) = \mathrm{e} ^ {- \delta t} h (t) x ^ {\gamma},\tag{19.45}
$$

where, because of the boundary conditions, we must demand that 

$$
h (T) = 0.\tag{19.46}
$$

Given a V of this form we have (using to denote the time derivative) 

$$
\frac {\partial V}{\partial t} = \mathrm{e} ^ {- \delta t} \dot {h} x ^ {\gamma} - \delta \mathrm{e} ^ {- \delta t} h x ^ {\gamma},\tag{19.47}
$$

$$
\frac {\partial V}{\partial x} = \gamma \mathrm{e} ^ {- \delta t} h x ^ {\gamma - 1},\tag{19.48}
$$

$$
\frac {\partial^ {2} V}{\partial x ^ {2}} = \gamma (\gamma - 1) \mathrm{e} ^ {- \delta t} h x ^ {\gamma - 2}.\tag{19.49}
$$

Inserting these expressions into (19.43)-(19.44) we get 

$$
\hat {\mathbf {w}} (t, \mathrm{x}) = \frac {a - r}{\sigma^ {2} (1 - \gamma)},\tag{19.50}
$$

$$
\hat {\mathbf {c}} (t, x) = x h (t) ^ {- 1 / (1 - \gamma)}.\tag{19.51}
$$

This looks very promising: we see that the candidate optimal portfolio is constant and that the candidate optimal consumption rule is linear in the wealth variable. In order to use the verification theorem we now want to show that a V-function of the form (19.45) actually solves the HJB equation. We therefore substitute the expressions (19.47)-(19.51) into the HJB equation. This gives us the equation 

$$
x ^ {\gamma} \left\{\dot {h} (t) + A h (t) + B h (t) ^ {- \gamma / (1 - \gamma)} \right\} = 0,
$$

where the constants A and B are given by 

$$
\begin{array}{l} A = \frac {\gamma (\alpha - r) ^ {2}}{\sigma^ {2} (1 - \gamma)} + r \gamma - \frac {1}{2} \frac {\gamma (\alpha - r) ^ {2}}{\sigma^ {2} (1 - \gamma)} - \delta \\ B = 1 - \gamma . \end{array}
$$

If this equation is to hold for all x and all t, then we see that h must solve the ODE 

$$
\dot {h} (t) + A h (t) + B h (t) ^ {- \gamma / (1 - \gamma)} = 0,\tag{19.52}
$$

$$
h (T) = 0.\tag{19.53}
$$

# THE MUTUAL FUND THEOREMS

An equation of this kind is known as a Bernoulli equation, and it can be solved explicitly (see the exercises). 

Summing up, we have shown that if we define V as in (19.45) with h defined as the solution to (19.52)-(19.53), and if we define w and 2 by (19.50)-(19.51), then V satisfies the HJB equation, and $\hat { \mathbf { w } } , \hat { \mathbf { c } }$ attain the supremum in the equation. The verification theorem then tells us that we have indeed found the optimal solution. 

## 19.7 The Mutual Fund Theorems

In this section we will briefly go through the "Merton mutual fund theorems", originally presented in Merton (1971). 

## 19.7.1 The Case with No Risk h e Asset

We consider a financial market with n asset prices $\displaystyle S _ { 1 } , \ldots , S _ { n }$ To start with we do not assume the existence of a risk free asset, and we assume that the price vector process $S ( t )$ has the following dynamics under the objective measure P. 

$$
\mathrm{d} S = D (S) \alpha \mathrm{d} t + D (S) \sigma \mathrm{d} W.\tag{19.54}
$$

Here W is a k-dimensional standard Wiener process, a is an n-vector, a is an n x k matrix, and $D ( S )$ is the diagonal matrix 

$$
D (S) = \operatorname{diag} [ S _ {1}, \dots , S _ {n} ].
$$

In more pedestrian terms this means that 

$$
\mathrm{d} S _ {i} = S _ {i} \alpha_ {i} \mathrm{d} t + S _ {i} \sigma_ {i} \mathrm{d} W,
$$

where $\sigma _ { i }$ is the ith row of the matrix $\sigma .$ 

We denote the investment strategy (relative portfolio) by w, and the consumption plan by c. If the pair (w, c) is self-financing, then it follows from the S-dynamics above, and from Lemma 6.4, that the dynamics of the wealth process X are given by 

$$
\mathrm{d} X = \mathrm {Xw^ {\prime} a dt - cdt+ Xw^ {\prime} \sigma dW}.\tag{19.55}
$$

We also take as given an instantaneous utility function $F ( t , \mathrm { c } )$ , and we basically want to maximize 

$$
E \left[ \int_ {0} ^ {T} F (t, c _ {t}) \mathrm{d} t \right],
$$

where T is some given time horizon. In order not to formulate a degenerate problem we also impose the condition that wealth is not allowed to become negative, and as before this is dealt with by introducing the stopping time 

$$
\dot {\tau} = \inf \left\{t > 0 \mid X _ {t} = 0 \right\} \wedge T.
$$

Our formal problem is then that of maximizing 

$$
E \left[ \int_ {0} ^ {\tau} F (t, c _ {t}) \mathrm{d} t \right]
$$

given the dynamics (19.54)-(19.55), and subject to the control constraints 

$$
\sum_ {1} ^ {n} w _ {i} = 1,\tag{19.56}
$$

$$
c \geq 0.\tag{19.57}
$$

Instead of (19.56) it is convenient to write 

$$
e ^ {\prime} w = 1,
$$

where e is the vector in $\mathbf { R } ^ { \mathrm { n } }$ which has the number 1 in all components, i.e. $e ^ { \prime } = ( 1 , \ldots , 1 )$ 

The HJB equation for this problem now becomes 

$$
\left\{ \begin{array}{l l} \frac {\partial V}{\partial t} (t, x, s) + \sup _ {e ^ {\prime} w = 1, c \geq 0} \{F (t, c) + \mathcal {A} ^ {c, w} V (t, x, s) \} = 0, \\ \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad V (T, x, s) = 0, \\ \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad V (t, 0, s) = 0. \end{array} \right.
$$

In the general case, when the parameters a and u are allowed to be functions of the price vector process S, the term $\boldsymbol { \mathcal { A } } ^ { c , w } V ( t , \boldsymbol { x } , \mathrm { s } )$ turns out to be rather forbidding (see Merton's original paper). It will in fact involve partial derivatives to the second order with respect to all the variables $\mathrm { x } , \pmb { \mathscr { s } } _ { 1 } , \ldots , \pmb { \mathscr { s } } _ { n }$ 

If, however, we assume that a and u are deterministic and constant over time, then we see by inspection that the wealth process X is a Markov process, and since the price processes do not appear, neither in the objective function nor in the definition of the stopping time, we draw the conclusion that in this case X itself will act as the state process, and we may forget about the underlying S-process completely. 

Under these assumptions we may thus write the optimal value function as $V ( \pmb { t } , \mathbf { x } )$ , with no s-dependence, and after some easy calculations the term ${ \mathbf { } } A ^ { c , w } V$ turns out to be 

$$
\mathcal {A} ^ {c, w} V = \mathbf {x} \mathbf {w} ^ {\prime} a \frac {\partial V}{\partial x} - c \frac {\partial V}{\partial x} + \frac {1}{2} x ^ {2} \mathbf {w} ^ {\prime} C \mathbf {w} \frac {\mathrm{a} ^ {2} \mathrm{V}}{\partial x ^ {2}},
$$

where the matrix $\Sigma$ is given by 

$$
\Sigma = \sigma \sigma^ {\prime}.
$$

We now summarize our assumptions. 

Assumption 19.7.1 We assume that 

the vector o is constant and deterministic 

the matrix a is constant and deterministic, 

the matrix u has rank n, and i n particular the matrix $\Sigma = \sigma \sigma ^ { \prime }$ is positive definite and invertible. 

We note that, in terms of contingent claims analysis, the last assumption means that the market is complete. Denoting partial derivatives by subscripts we now have the following HJB equation 

$$
\left\{ \begin{array}{l l} V _ {t} (t, x) + \sup _ {w ^ {\prime} e = 1, c \geq 0} \big \{F (t, c) + (x w ^ {\prime} \alpha - c) V _ {x} (t, \mathrm{x}) + \frac {1}{2} x ^ {2} w ^ {\prime} \Sigma w V _ {x x} (t, x) \big \} = \mathbf {0}, \\ V (T, x) = 0, \\ V (t, 0) = 0. \end{array} \right.
$$

If we relax the constraint $\mathrm { w e } \ = \ 1$ , the Lagrange function for the static optimization problem is given by 

$$
\mathrm{L} = F (t, c) + (x w ^ {\prime} \alpha - c) V _ {x} (t, x) + \frac {1}{2} x ^ {2} w ^ {\prime} \Sigma w V _ {x x} (t, \mathrm{x}) + \lambda (1 - \mathrm {w^ {\prime} e})
$$

Assuming the problem to be regular enough for an interior solution we see that the first order condition for c is 

$$
\frac {\partial F}{\partial c} (t, c) = V _ {x} (t, x).
$$

The first order condition for w is 

$$
x \alpha^ {\prime} V _ {x} + x ^ {2} V _ {x x} w ^ {\prime} \Sigma = \lambda e ^ {\prime},
$$

so we can solve for w in order to obtain 

$$
\hat {w} = \Sigma^ {- 1} \left[ \frac {\lambda}{x ^ {2} V _ {x x}} e - \frac {x V _ {x}}{x ^ {2} V _ {x x}} \alpha \right].\tag{19.58}
$$

Using the relation e'w = 1 this gives X as 

$$
\lambda = \frac {x ^ {2} V _ {x x} + x V _ {x} e ^ {\prime} \Sigma^ {- 1} \alpha}{e ^ {\prime} \Sigma^ {- 1} e},
$$

and inserting this into (19.58) gives us, after some manipulation, 

$$
\dot {\boldsymbol {w}} = \frac {1}{e ^ {\prime} \Sigma^ {- 1} e} \Sigma^ {- 1} e + \frac {V _ {x}}{x V _ {x x}} \Sigma^ {- 1} \left[ \frac {e ^ {\prime} \Sigma^ {- 1} \alpha}{e ^ {\prime} \Sigma^ {- 1} e} e - \alpha \right].\tag{19.59}
$$

To see more clearly what is going on we can write this expression as 

$$
\hat {\mathbf {w}} (t) = g + Y (t) h,\tag{19.60}
$$

where the fixed vectors g and h are given by 

$$
g = \frac {1}{e ^ {\prime} \Sigma^ {- 1} e} \Sigma^ {- 1} e,\tag{19.61}
$$

$$
h = \Sigma^ {- 1} \left[ \frac {e ^ {\prime} \Sigma^ {- 1} \alpha}{e ^ {\prime} \Sigma^ {- 1} e} e - \alpha \right],\tag{19.62}
$$

whereas Y is given by 

$$
Y (t) = \frac {V _ {x} (t , X (t))}{X (t) V _ {x x} (t , X (t))}.\tag{19.63}
$$

Thus we see that the optimal portfolio is moving stochastically along the o n e dimensional "optimal portfolio line" 

$$
g + s h,
$$

in the $( n - 1 )$ )-dimensional "portfolio hyperplane" A, where 

$$
\Delta = \{w \in R ^ {n} \mid e ^ {\prime} w = 1 \}.
$$

We now make the obvious geometric observation that if we fix two points on the optimal portfolio line, say the points $\mathbf { w ^ { a } } = \mathbf { g } ^ { + }$ ah and $\mathbf { w } ^ { \mathrm { b } } = \mathbf { g }$ + bh, then any point w on the line can be written as an f i n e combination of the basis points ${ \bf w } ^ { \mathbf { a } }$ and $\mathrm { w } ^ { \mathrm { b } }$ . An easy calculation shows that if $w ^ { \pm } = \pmb { g } ^ { + }$ sh then we can write 

$$
w ^ {s} = \mu w ^ {a} + (1 - \mu) w ^ {b},
$$

where 

$$
\mu = \frac {s - b}{a - b},
$$

The point of all this is that we now have an interesting economic interpretation of the optimality results above. Let us thus fix $\mathbf { W } ^ { \mathbf { a } }$ and $\mathrm { ^ { - } w ^ { b } }$ as above on the optimal portfolio line. Since these points are in the portfolio plane A we can interpret them as the relative portfolios of two fixed mutual funds. We may then write (19.60) as 

$$
\hat {\mathbf {w}} (t) = \mu (t) w ^ {a} + (1 - \mu (t)) w ^ {b},\tag{19.64}
$$

with 

$$
\mu (t) = \frac {\mathrm{Y} (t) - b}{a - \bar {b}}.
$$

Thus we see that the optimal portfolio w can be obtained as aUsuper portfolio" where we allocate resources between two fixed mutual funds. 

'heorem 19.9 (Mutual fund theorem) Assume that the problem is regular nough to allow for an interior solution. Then there exists a one-dimensional urameterized family of mutual funds, given by $\mathrm { w } ^ { \mathrm { s } } = g + s h$ , where g and h are efined by (1 9.62)-(19.62), such that the following hold: 

1. For each fied s the relative portfolio $\mathbf { w } ^ { s }$ stays fied over time. 

2. For any fied choice of a $\neq b$ the optimal portfolio w(t) is, for all values of t, obtained by allocating a11 resources between the fied funds ${ \bf w } ^ { \mathbf { a } }$ and $w ^ { b }$ , i.e. 

$$
\begin{array}{r} \hat {\mathbf {w}} (t) = \mu^ {a} (t) w ^ {a} + \mu^ {b} (t) w ^ {b}, \\ \mu^ {a} (t) + \mathrm{p} ^ {\mathrm{b}} (\mathrm{t}) = 1. \end{array}
$$

3. The relative proportions $( \boldsymbol { \mathrm { p } } ^ { \mathrm { a } } , \boldsymbol { \mathrm { p } } ^ { \mathrm { b } } )$ of the portfolio wealth allocated to $w ^ { \pmb { \alpha } }$ and $\mathrm { w } ^ { \mathrm { b } }$ respectively are given by 

$$
\mu^ {a} (t) = \frac {Y (t) - b}{a - b},
$$

$$
\mu^ {b} (t) = \frac {\mathrm{a} - Y (\mathrm{t})}{a - b},
$$

where Y is given by (19.65'). 

## 19.7.2 The Case with a Risk flee Asset

Again we consider the model 

$$
\mathrm{d} S = D (S) \alpha \mathrm{dt} + D (S) \sigma \mathrm{d} W (t),\tag{19.65}
$$

with the same assumptions as in the preceding section. We now also take as given the standard risk free asset B with dynamics 

$$
\mathrm{dB} = r B \mathrm{dt}.
$$

Formally we can denote this as a new asset by subscript zero, i.e. $\mathbf { B } = \mathbf { S } \mathbf { o } ,$ , and then we can consider relative portfolios of the form $\mathbf { w } = ( w _ { 0 } , w _ { 1 } , \dots , w _ { n } ) ^ { \prime }$ where of course $\begin{array} { r } { \sum _ { 0 } ^ { n } w _ { i } = 1 } \end{array}$ . Since B will play such a special role it will, however, be convenient to eliminate ${ \pmb w } _ { 0 }$ by the relation 

$$
w _ {0} = 1 - \sum_ {1} ^ {n} w _ {i},
$$

and then use the letter w to denote the portfolio weight vector for the risky assets only. Thus we use the notation 

$$
\mathrm{w} = (w _ {1}, \dots , w _ {n}) ^ {\prime},
$$

and we note that this truncated portfolio vector is allowed to take any value in $R ^ { n }$ . 

Given this notation it is easily seen that the dynamics of a self-financing portfolio are given by 

$$
\mathrm{d} X = X \cdot \left\{\sum_ {1} ^ {n} w _ {i} \alpha_ {i} + \left(1 - \sum_ {1} ^ {n} w _ {i}\right) r \right\} \mathrm{d} t - c \mathrm{d} t + X \cdot w ^ {\prime} \sigma \mathrm{d} W.
$$

That is, 

$$
\mathrm{d} X = X \cdot w ^ {\prime} (\alpha - r e) \mathrm{d} t + (r X - c) \mathrm{d} t + X \cdot w ^ {\prime} \sigma \mathrm{d} W,\tag{19.66}
$$

where as before $e \in \mathbf { R } ^ { \mathrm { n } }$ denotes the vector $( 1 , 1 , \ldots , 1 ) ^ { \prime }$ 

The HJB equation now becomes 

$$
\left\{ \begin{array}{l l} V _ {t} (t, x) + \sup _ {c \geq 0,   w \in R ^ {n}} \{F (t, c) + \mathcal {A} ^ {c, w} V (t, x) \} = 0, \\ & V (T, x) = 0, \\ & V (t, 0) = 0, \end{array} \right.
$$

where 

$$
\mathcal {A} ^ {c} V = x w ^ {\prime} (\alpha - r e) V _ {x} (t, x) + (r x - c) V _ {x} (t, x) + \frac {1}{2} x ^ {2} w ^ {\prime} \Sigma w V _ {x x} (t, x).
$$

The first order conditions for the static optimization problem are 

$$
\frac {\partial F}{\partial \boldsymbol {c}} (\boldsymbol {t}, \boldsymbol {c}) = V _ {\boldsymbol {x}} (t, \boldsymbol {x}),
$$

$$
\hat {w} = - \frac {V _ {\underline {{x}}}}{x V _ {x x}} \Sigma^ {- 1} (\alpha - r e),
$$

and again we have a geometrically obvious economic interpretation. 

Theorem 19.10 (Mutual fund theorem) Given assumptions as above, the following hold: 

1. The optimal portfolio consists of an allocation between two fied mutual funds $\mathbf { \Delta } _ { w } \mathbf { 0 }$ and wf. 

2. The fund $w ^ { 0 }$ consists only of the risk free asset. 

3. The fund wf consists only of the risky assets, and is given by 

$$
w ^ {f} = \Sigma^ {- 1} (\alpha - r e).
$$

4. At each t the optimal relative allocation of wealth between the funds is given by 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \mu^ {f} (t) = - \frac {V _ {x} (t , X (t))}{X (t) V _ {x x} (t , X (t))}, \\ \mu^ {0} (t) = 1 - \mu^ {f} (\mathrm{t}). \end{array}
$$

Note that this result is not a corollary of the corresponding result from the previous section. Firstly it was an essential ingredient in the previous results that the volatility matrix of the price vector was invertible. In the case with a riskless asset the volatility matrix for the entire price vector $( \mathbf { B } , S _ { 1 } , \ldots , S _ { n } )$ is of course degenerate, since its first row (having subscript zero) is identically equal to zero. Secondly, even if one assumes the results from the previous section, i.e. that the optimal portfolio is built up from two fixed portfolios, it is not at all obvious that one of these basis portfolios can be chosen so as to consist of the risk free asset alone.
