## 24.4 Forward Measures

In this section we specialize the theory developed in the previous section to the case when the new numeraire chosen is a bond maturing at time T. As can be expected this choice of numeraire is particularly useful when dealing with interest rate derivatives. 

## 24.4.1 Using the T-bond as Numeraire

Suppose that we are given a specified bond market model with a fixed (money account) martingale measure Q. For a fixed time ot maturity T we now choose the zero coupon bond maturing at T as our new numeraire. 

Definition 24.6 For a fixed T, the T-forward measure $Q ^ { T }$ is defined as the martingale measure for the numeraire process $p ( t , T )$ 

In interest rate theory we often have our models specified under the risk neutral martingale measure Q with the money account B as the numeraire. We then have the following explicit description $\mathbf { \bar { \boldsymbol { Q } } } ^ { T }$ 

Proposition 24.7 If Q denotes the risk neutral martingale measure, then the likelihood process 

$$
L ^ {T} (t) = \frac {\mathrm{d} Q ^ {T}}{\mathrm{d} Q}, \quad o n \mathcal {F} _ {t}, 0 \leq t \leq T
$$

is given by 

$$
L ^ {T} (t) = \frac {p (t , T)}{B (t) p (0 , T)}.\tag{24.21}
$$

In particular, if the Q-dynamics of the T-bond are Wiener driven, i.e. of the form 

$$
\mathrm{d} p (t, T) = r (t) p (t, T) \mathrm{d} t + p (t, T) v (t, T) \mathrm{d} W (t),\tag{24.22}
$$

where W is a (possibly multidimensional) Q Wiener process, then the $L ^ { T }$ dynamics are given by 

$$
\mathrm{d} L ^ {T} (t) = L ^ {T} (t) v (t, T) \mathrm{d} W (t),\tag{24.23}
$$

i.e. the Girsanov kernel for the transition from Q to $Q ^ { T }$ is given by the T-bond volatility ${ \pmb v } ( { \pmb t } , T )$ 

Proof The result follows immediately from Proposition 24.4 with $Q ^ { T } = \underset { \longmapsto } { Q ^ { 1 } }$ and $Q ^ { 0 } = Q$ 

Observing that $P ( T , T ) = I$ we have the following useful pricing formula as an immediate corollary of Proposition 24.2. 

Proposition 24.8 For any T-claim X we have 

$$
\boldsymbol {\Pi} (t; X) = \boldsymbol {p} (t, T) E ^ {T} [ X | \mathcal {F} _ {t} ],\tag{24.24}
$$

where $E ^ { T }$ denotes integration w.r.t. $Q ^ { T }$ 

Note again that the price ${ \pmb p } ( t , T )$ does not have to be computed. It can be observed directly on the market at time t. 

A natural question to ask is when Q and $Q ^ { T }$ coincide. 

Lemma 24.9 The relation $Q = Q ^ { T }$ holds if and only if r is deterministic. 

Proof Exercise for the reader. 

# FORWARD MEASURES

## 24.4.2 An Expectation Hypothesis

We now make a small digression to discuss the forward rate process f (t, T). The economic interpretation of f (t, T) is that this is the risk free rate of return which we may have on an investment over the infinitesimal interval $[ \mathrm { T } , \mathrm { T } + \mathrm { d } T ]$ if the contract is made at t. On the other hand, the short rate $r ( T )$ is the risk free rate of return over the infinitesimal interval $[ \mathrm { T } , \mathrm { T } + \mathrm { d } T ]$ , if the contract is made at T. Thus it is natural to view $\mathbf { f } \left( \mathbf { t } , \mathrm { T } \right)$ (which can be observed at t) as an estimate of the future short rate $r ( T )$ . More explicitly it is sometimes argued that if the market expects the short rate at T to be high, then it seems reasonable to assume that the forward rate f (t, T ) is also high, since otherwise there would be profits to be made on the bond market. 

Our task now is to determine whether this reawning is correct in a more p r e cise sense, and to this end we study the most formalized version of the argument above, known as the "unbiased expectation hypothesis" for forward rates. This hypothesis then says that in an efficient market we must have 

$$
f (t, T) = E [ r (T) | \mathcal {F} _ {t} ],\tag{24.25}
$$

i.e. the present forward rate is an unbiased estimator of the future spot rate. If we interpret the expression "an efficient market" as "an arbitrage free market" then we may use our general machinery to analyze the problem. 

First we notice that there is no probability measure indicated in (24.25), so we have to make a choice. 

Of course there is no reason at all to expect the hypothesis to be true under the objective measure $\mathbf { P } ,$ but it is often claimed that it holds "in a risk neutral world". This more refined version of the hypothesis can then be formulated as 

$$
f (t, T) = E ^ {Q} [ r (T) | \mathcal {F} _ {t} ],\tag{24.26}
$$

where Q is the usual risk neutral martingale measure. In fact, also this version of the expectation hypothesis is in general incorrect, which is shown by the following result. 

Lemma 24.10 Assume that, for all $\mathbf T > 0$ we have $r ( T ) / B ( T ) \in L ^ { 1 } ( \mathrm { Q } )$ ). Then, for every jixed T, the process $\mathbf { f } \left( \mathbf { t } , \mathbf { T } \right)$ is a $\mathbf { Q } ^ { \mathrm { { T } } }$ -martingale for $0 \leq t \leq \mathrm { T }$ , and in particular we have 

$$
f (t, T) = E ^ {T} [ r (T) | \mathcal {F} _ {t} ].\tag{24.27}
$$

Proof Using Proposition 24.24 with $X = r ( T )$ we have 

$$
\Pi (t; \mathrm{X}) = E ^ {Q} \left[ r (T) \mathrm{e} ^ {- \int_ {t} ^ {T} r (s) \mathrm{d} s} \mid \mathcal {F} _ {t} \right] = p (t, T) E ^ {T} [ r (T) | \mathcal {F} _ {t} ].
$$

This gives us 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} E ^ {T} [ r (T) | \mathcal {F} _ {t} ] & = \frac {}{p (t , T)} E ^ {Q} \left[ r (T) \mathrm{e} ^ {- \int_ {t} ^ {T} r (s) \mathrm{d} s} \right| \mathcal {F} _ {t} \\ & = - \frac {1}{p (t , T)} E ^ {Q} \left[ \frac {\partial}{\partial T} \mathrm{e} ^ {- \int_ {t} ^ {T} r (s) \mathrm{d} s} \right| \mathcal {F} _ {t} \\ & = - \frac {1}{p (t , T)} \frac {\partial}{- 1} E ^ {Q} \left[ \mathrm{e} ^ {- \int_ {t} ^ {T} r (s) \mathrm{d} s} \right| \mathcal {F} _ {t} \\ & = - \frac {}{p (t , T)} = f (t, T). \end{array}
$$

We thus see that the expectation hypothesis is false also under $\scriptstyle Q ,$ but true under $Q ^ { T }$ . Note, however, that we have different $Q ^ { T }$ for different choices of the maturity date T. 

## 24.5 A General Option Pricing Formula

The object of this section is to give a fairly general formula for the pricing of European call options, and for the rest of the section we basically follow Geman et al. (1995). Assume therefore that we are given a financial market with a (possibly stochastic) short rate r , and a strictly positive asset price process $S ( t )$ 

The option under consideration is a European call on $s$ with date of maturity T and strike price K. We are thus considering the T-claim 

$$
\mathrm{X} = \max [ S (T) - K, 0 ],\tag{24.28}
$$

and, for readability reasons, we confine ourselves to computing the option price $\Pi ( t ; \mathrm { X } )$ at time $\mathbf { t } = 0$ 

The main reason for the existence of a large number of explicit option pricing formulas is that the contract function for an option is piecewise linear. We can capitalize on this fact by using a not so well-known trick with indicator functions. Write the option as 

$$
\mathcal {X} = [ S (T) - K ] \cdot I \{S (T) \geq K \},
$$

where I is the indicator function, i.e. 

$$
I \left\{S (T) \geq K \right\} = \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} 1 & \text { if } S (T) \geq K, \\ 0 & \text { if } S (T) <   K. \end{array} \right.
$$

Denoting the risk neutral martingale measure by $Q , \mathrm { w e }$ obtain 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} \Pi (0; \mathcal {X}) & = E ^ {Q} \left[ B ^ {- 1} (T) [ S (T) - K ] I \{S (T) \geq K \} \right] \\ & = E ^ {Q} \left[ \mathrm{e} ^ {- \int_ {0} ^ {T} r (s) \mathrm{d} s} S (T) \cdot I \{S (T) \geq K \} \right] \\ & \quad - K E ^ {Q} \left[ \mathrm{e} ^ {- \int_ {0} ^ {T} r (s) \mathrm{d} s} \cdot I \{S (T) \geq K \} \right]. \end{array}
$$

In the first term above, we use the measure $Q ^ { s }$ having S as numeraire, and for the second term we use the T-forward measure. From Theorem 24.2 and Proposition 24.8 we then obtain the following basic option pricing formula, which is a substantial extension of the standard Black-Scholes formula. 

Proposition 24.11 (General option pricing formula) Given the assumptions above, the option price is given by 

$$
\Pi (0; \mathcal {X}) = S (0) Q ^ {S} (S (T) \geq K) - K p (0, T) Q ^ {T} (S (T) \geq K).\tag{24.29}
$$

Here $\boldsymbol { \mathrm { Q ^ { T } } }$ denotes the T-forward measure, whereas $Q ^ { S }$ denotes the martingale measure for the numemire process $S ( t )$ 

In order to use this formula in a real situation we have to be able to compute the probabilities above, and the standard condition which ensures computability turns out to be that volatilities should be deterministic. Hence we have the following &sumption. 

Assumption 24.5.1 Assume that the process $\boldsymbol { z } _ { s , T }$ ~ defined by 

$$
Z _ {S, T} (t) = \frac {S (t)}{p (t , T)}\tag{24.30}
$$

has a stochastic differential of the form 

$$
\mathrm{d} Z _ {S, T} (t) = Z _ {S, T} (t) m _ {S, T} (t) \mathrm{d} t + Z _ {S, T} (t) \sigma_ {S, T} (t) \mathrm{d} W (t),\tag{24.31}
$$

where the volatility process $\sigma _ { S , T } ( t )$ ) is deterministic. 

The crucial point here is of course the assumption that the row-vector process $\boldsymbol { \sigma } _ { \boldsymbol { S } , T }$ ~ is deterministic. Note that the volatility process as always is unaffected by a change of measure, so we do not have to specify under which measure we check the condition. It can be done under P as well as under Q. 

We start the computations by writing the probability in the second term of (24.29) as 

$$
Q ^ {T} (S (T) \geq K) = Q ^ {T} \left(\frac {S (T)}{p (T , T)} \geq K\right) = Q ^ {T} (Z _ {S, T} (T) \geq K).\tag{24.32}
$$

Since $\boldsymbol { Z } _ { \boldsymbol { S } , T }$ ~ is an asset price, normalized by the price of a T-bond, it is a $Q ^ { T }$ martingale, so its $\boldsymbol { \mathrm { Q ^ { T } } }$ -dynamics are given by 

$$
\mathrm{d} Z _ {S, T} (t) = Z _ {S, T} (t) \sigma_ {S, T} (t) \mathrm{d} W ^ {T} (t).\tag{24.33}
$$

This is basically GBM, driven by a multidimensional Wiener process, and it is easy to see that the solution is given by 

$$
Z _ {S, T} (T) = \frac {S (0)}{p (0 , T)} \exp \left\{- \frac {1}{2} \int_ {0} ^ {T} \| \sigma_ {S, T} \| ^ {2} (t) \mathrm{d} t + \int_ {0} ^ {T} \sigma_ {S, T} (t) \mathrm{d} W ^ {T} (t) \right\}.\tag{24.34}
$$

In the exponent we have a stochastic integral and a deterministic time integral. Since the integrand in the stochastic integral is deterministic, an easy extension of Lemma 4.15 shows that the stochastic integral has a Gaussian distribution with zero mean and variance 

$$
\Sigma_ {S, T} ^ {2} (T) = \int_ {0} ^ {T} \| \sigma_ {S, T} (t) \| ^ {2} d t.\tag{24.35}
$$

The entire exponent is thus normally distributed, and we can write the probability in the second term in (24.29) as 

$$
Q ^ {T} (S (T) \geq K) = N [ d _ {2} ],
$$

where 

$$
d _ {2} = \frac {\ln (S (0) / K p (0 , T)) - \frac {1}{2} \Sigma_ {S , T} ^ {2} (T)}{\sqrt {\Sigma_ {S , T} ^ {2} (T)}}.\tag{24.36}
$$

Since the first probability term in (24.29) is a $Q ^ { s } .$ -probability, it is natural to write the event under consideration in terms of a quotient with $s$ in the denominator. Thus we write 

$$
Q ^ {S} (S (T) \geq K) = Q ^ {S} \left. \left(\overline {{Y}} ^ {T} T\right) ^ {\bullet} \leq \frac {1}{K}\right) = Q ^ {S} \left(Y _ {S, T} (T) \leq \frac {1}{K}\right),\tag{24.37}
$$

where $Y _ { S , T }$ is defined by 

$$
Y _ {S, T} (t) = \frac {p (t , T)}{S (t)} = \frac {1}{Z _ {S , T} (t)}.
$$

Under $\boldsymbol { \mathrm { Q } } ^ { \mathrm { s } }$ the process $Y _ { S , T }$ has zero drift, so its $Q ^ { s }$ -dynamics are of the form 

$$
\mathrm{d} Y _ {S, T} (t) = Y _ {S, T} (t) \delta_ {S, T} (t) \mathrm{d} W ^ {S} (t).
$$

Since $Y _ { S , T } = Z _ { S , T } ^ { - 1 }$ , an easy application of I~B'S formula gives us $\delta _ { S , T } ( t ) =$ $- \sigma _ { S , T } ( t )$ . Thus we have 

$$
Y _ {S, T} (T) = \frac {p (0 , T)}{S (0)} \exp \left\{- \frac {1}{2} \int_ {0} ^ {T} \| \sigma_ {S, T} \| ^ {2} (t) d t - \int_ {0} ^ {T} \sigma_ {S, T} (t) d W ^ {S} \right\},
$$

and again we have a normally distributed exponent. Thus, after some simplification, 

$$
Q ^ {S} (S (T) \supseteq K) = N [ d _ {1} ],
$$

where 

$$
d _ {1} = d _ {2} + \sqrt {\Sigma_ {S , T} ^ {2} (T)}.\tag{24.38}
$$

We have thus proved the following result. 

Proposition 24.12 (Geman-El Karoui-Rochet) Under the conditions given in Assumption 24.5.1, the price of the call option defined in (24.28) is given by the formula 

$$
\Pi (0; \mathcal {X}) = S (0) N [ d _ {1} ] - K \cdot p (0, T) N [ d _ {2} ].\tag{24.39}
$$

Here $d _ { 2 }$ and $d _ { 1 }$ are given in (24.36) and (24.38), respectively, whereas $\Sigma _ { S , T } ^ { 2 } ( T )$ is defined by (24.35). 

## 24.6 T h e Hull- White Model

As a concrete application of the option pricing formula of the previous section, we will now consider the case of interest rate options in the Hull-White model (extended VasiEek). To this end recall that in the Hull-White model the Q-dynamics of r are given by 

$$
d r = \left\{\Phi (t) - a r\right) \mathrm{dt} + \sigma \mathrm{d} W.\tag{24.40}
$$

From Section 22.3 we recall that we have an affine term structure 

$$
p (t, T) = \mathrm{e} ^ {A (t, T) - B (t, T) r (t)},\tag{24.41}
$$

where A and B are deterministic functions, and where B is given by 

$$
B (t, T) = \frac {1}{a} \left\{1 - \mathrm{e} ^ {- a (T - t)} \right\}.\tag{24.42}
$$

The project is to price a European call option with exercise date $\pmb { T _ { 1 } }$ and strike price K, on an underlying bond with date of maturity $\pmb { T _ { 2 } }$ , where $T _ { 1 } < T _ { 2 }$ In the notation of the general theory above this means that $\mathrm { T } = T _ { 1 }$ and that ${ \cal S } ( t ) = p ( t , T _ { 2 } )$ . We start by checking Assumption 24.5.1, i.e. if the volatility, $\sigma _ { z }$ of the process 

$$
Z (t) = \frac {p (t T _ {2})}{p (t , T _ {1})}\tag{24.43}
$$

is deterministic. (In terms of the notation in Section 24.5 Z corresponds to $\pmb { Z } _ { \pmb { S } , \pmb { T } }$ and $\sigma _ { z }$ corresponds to $\sigma _ { S , T } . )$ 

Inserting (24.41) into (24.43) gives 

$$
Z (t) = \exp \left\{A (t, T _ {2}) - A (t, T _ {1}) - [ B (t, T _ {2}) - B (t, T _ {1}) ] r (t) \right\}.
$$

Applying the It6 formula to this expression, and using (24.40), we get the Q-dynamics 

$$
\mathrm{d} Z (t) = Z (t) \{\dots . \} \mathrm{dt} + Z (t). \sigma_ {z} (\mathrm{t}) \mathrm{d} W,\tag{24.44}
$$

where 

$$
\sigma_ {z} (t) = - \sigma [ B (t, T _ {2}) - B (t, T _ {1}) ] = \frac {\sigma}{a} \mathrm{e} ^ {a t} [ \mathrm{e} ^ {- a T _ {2}} - \mathrm{e} ^ {- a T _ {1}} ].\tag{24.45}
$$

Thus $\mathbf { a } ,$ is in fact deterministic, so we may apply Proposition 24.12. We obtain the following result, which also holds (why?) for the VasiEek model. 

Proposition 24.13 (Hull-White bond option) In the Hull-White model $( 2 4 . 4 0 )$ the price, at $t = 0$ , of a European call with strike price K , and time of maturity $\pmb { T _ { 1 } }$ I, o n a bond maturing at $T _ { 2 }$ is given by the formula 

$$
\Pi (0; \mathcal {X}) = p (0, T _ {2}) N [ d _ {1} ] - K \cdot p (0, T _ {1}) N [ d _ {2} ],\tag{24.46}
$$

where 

$$
d _ {2} = \frac {\ln \left(p (0 , T _ {2}) / K p (0 , T _ {1})\right) - \frac {1}{2} \Sigma^ {2}}{\sqrt {\Sigma^ {2}}},\tag{24.47}
$$

$$
d _ {1} = d _ {2} + \sqrt {\Sigma^ {2}},\tag{24.48}
$$

$$
\Sigma^ {2} = \frac {\sigma^ {2}}{2 a ^ {3}} \left\{1 - \mathrm{e} ^ {- 2 a T _ {1}} \right\} \left\{1 - \mathrm{e} ^ {- a (T _ {2} - T _ {1})} \right\} ^ {2}.\tag{24.49}
$$

We end the discussion of the Hull-White model, by studying the pricing problem for a claim of the form 

$$
\mathcal {Z} = \Phi (r (T)).
$$

Using the T-bond as numeraire Proposition 24.8 gives us 

$$
\Pi (t; \mathcal {Z}) = p (t, T) E ^ {T} [ \Phi (r (T)) | \mathcal {F} _ {t} ],\tag{24.50}
$$

so we must find the distribution of $r ( T )$ under $\boldsymbol { \mathrm { Q ^ { T } } }$ , and to this end we will use Theorem 24.5 (with Q as $Q ^ { 0 }$ and $\mathrm { Q ^ { \mathrm { T } } }$ as ${ \bf Q ^ { 1 } } )$ . We thus need the volatility of the T-bond, and from (24.41)-(24.42) we obtain bond prices (under Q) as 

$$
\mathrm{d} p (t, T) = r (t) p (t, T) \mathrm{d} t + v (t, T) p (t, T) \mathrm{d} W,\tag{24.51}
$$

where the volatility $v ( t , \mathrm { T } )$ is given by 

$$
v (t, \mathrm{T}) = - \sigma B (t, \mathrm{T}).\tag{24.52}
$$

Thus, using Theorem 24.5 and the fact that the money account B has zero volatility, the Girsanov kernel for the transition from Q to $\mathrm { Q ^ { \mathrm { T } } }$ is given by 

$$
\varphi^ {T} (t) = - \sigma B (t, T).
$$

The $Q ^ { T }$ -dynamics of the short rate are thus given by 

$$
\mathrm{d} r = \left[ \Theta (t) - a r - \sigma^ {2} B (t, T) \right] \mathrm{d} t + \sigma \mathrm{d} W ^ {T},\tag{24.53}
$$

where $W ^ { T }$ is a $\boldsymbol { \mathrm { Q ^ { T } } }$ -Wiener process. 

We observe that, since $v ( t , \mathrm { T } )$ and $\Theta ( t )$ are deterministic, $\pmb { r }$ is a Gaussian process, so the distribution of $r ( T )$ is completely determined by its mean and variance under $\boldsymbol { \mathrm { Q } } ^ { \mathrm { T } }$ . Solving the linear SDE (24.53) gives us 

$$
\begin{array}{l} r (T) = \mathrm{e} ^ {- a (T - t)} + \int_ {t} ^ {T} \mathrm{e} ^ {- a (T - s)} [ \Theta (s) - \sigma^ {2} B (s, T) ] \mathrm{d} s \\ \qquad + \sigma \int_ {t} ^ {T} \mathrm{e} ^ {- a (T - s)} \mathrm{d} W ^ {T} (s). \end{array}\tag{24.54}
$$

We can now compute the conditional $\mathbf { Q } ^ { \mathrm { { T } } } { \cdot }$ -variance of $r ( T ) , \sigma _ { r } ^ { 2 } ( \mathrm { t } , \mathrm { T } )$ , as 

$$
\sigma_ {r} ^ {2} (t, T) = \sigma^ {2} \int_ {t} ^ {T} \mathrm{e} ^ {- 2 a (T - s)} \mathrm{d} s = \frac {\sigma^ {2}}{2 a} \left\{1 - \mathrm{e} ^ {- 2 a (T - t)} \right\}.\tag{24.55}
$$

Note that the $\mathrm { Q ^ { T }  – m e a n }$ of $r ( T ) , m _ { r } ( t , T ) = E ^ { T } \left\{ r ( T ) | \mathcal { F } _ { t } \right\}$ ], does not have to be computed at all. We obtain it directly from Lemma 24.10 as 

$$
m _ {r} (t, T) = f (t, T),
$$

which can be observed directly from market data. 

Under $\boldsymbol { \mathrm { Q ^ { T } } }$ , the conditional distribution of $r ( T )$ is thus the normal distribution $\mathrm { N } [ \mathrm { f } \left( \mathrm { t } , \mathrm { T } \right) , \sigma _ { r } ( t , T ) ]$ , and performing the integration in (24.50) we have the final result. 

Proposition 24.14 Given the assumptions above, the price of the claim $\mathbf { X } =$ $\Phi ( r ( T ) )$ ) is given by 

$$
\Pi (t; X) = p (t, T) \frac {1}{\sqrt {2 \pi \sigma_ {r} ^ {2} (t , T)}} \int_ {- \infty} ^ {\infty} \Phi (z) \exp \left\{- \frac {[ z - f (t , T) ] ^ {2}}{2 \sigma_ {r} ^ {2} (t , T)} \right\} d z,\tag{24.56}
$$

where $\sigma _ { r } ^ { 2 } ( t , T )$ is given by (24.55). 

## 24.7 The General Gaussian Model

In this section we extend our earlier results, by computing prices of bond options in a general Gaussian forward rate model. We specify the model (under Q) as 

$$
\mathrm{d} f (t, T) = \alpha (t, T) \mathrm{d} t + \sigma (t, T) \mathrm{d} W (t),\tag{24.57}
$$

where W is a d-dimensional Q-Wiener process. 

Assumption 24.7.1 We assume that the volatility vector function 

$$
\sigma (t, T) = [ \sigma_ {1} (t, T), \dots , \sigma_ {d} (t, T) ]
$$

is a deterministic function of the variables t and ${ \mathbf T } .$ 

Using Proposition 20.5 the bond price dynamics under Q are given by 

$$
\mathrm{d} p (t, T) = p (t, T) r (t) \mathrm{d} t + p (t, T) v (t, T) \mathrm{d} W (t),\tag{24.58}
$$

where the volatility is given by 

$$
v (t, T) = - \int_ {t} ^ {T} \sigma (t, s) \mathrm{d} s.\tag{24.59}
$$

We consider a European call option, with expiration date $T _ { 0 }$ and exercise price K, on an underlying bond with maturity $\pmb { T _ { 1 } }$ (where of course $T _ { 0 } < \mathrm { T } _ { \mathrm { I } } )$ . In order to compute the price of the bond, we use Proposition 24.12, which means that we first have to find the volatility $\sigma _ { T _ { 1 } , T _ { 0 } }$ T ~ of the process 

$$
Z (t) = \frac {p (t , T _ {1})}{p (t , \mathrm{To})}.
$$

An easy calculation shows that in fact 

$$
\sigma_ {T _ {1}, T _ {0}} (t) = v (t, T _ {1}) - v (t, T _ {0}) = - \int_ {T _ {0}} ^ {T _ {1}} \sigma (t, s) d s.\tag{24.60}
$$

This is clearly deterministic, so Assumption 24.5.1 is satisfied. We now have the following pricing formula. 

Proposition 24.15 (Option prices for Gaussian forward rates) The price, at $\mathbf { t } = \mathbf { 0 } .$ , of the option 

$$
\mathcal {X} = \max \left[ p (T _ {0}, T _ {1}) - K, 0 \right]
$$

is given by 

$$
\Pi (0; \mathcal {X}) = p (0, T _ {1}) N [ d _ {1} ] - K. p (0, T _ {0}) N [ d _ {2} ],\tag{24.61}
$$

where 

$$
d _ {1} = \frac {\ln (p (0 , T _ {1}) / K p (0 , T _ {0})) + \frac {1}{2} \Sigma_ {T _ {1} , T _ {0}} ^ {2}}{\sqrt {\Sigma_ {T _ {1} , T _ {0}} ^ {2}}},
$$

$$
d _ {2} = d _ {1} - \sqrt {\Sigma_ {T _ {1} , T _ {0}} ^ {2}},
$$

$$
\Sigma_ {T _ {1}, T _ {0}} ^ {2} = \int_ {0} ^ {T _ {0}} \| \sigma_ {T _ {1}, T _ {0}} (s) \| ^ {2} d s,
$$

and $\sigma _ { T _ { 1 } , T _ { 0 } }$ is given by (24.60). 

Proof Follows immediately from Proposition 24.12. 

# CAPS AND FLOORS

## 24.8 Caps and Floors

The object of this section is to present one of the most traded of all interest rate derivatives-the c a p a n d to show how it can be priced. 

An interest rate cap is a financial insurance contract which protects you from having to pay more than a prespecified rate, the cap rate, even though you have a loan at a floating rate of interest. There are also floor contracts which guarantee that the interest paid on a floating rate loan will never be below some predetermined floor rate. For simplicity we assume that we are standing at time t = 0, and that the cap is to be in force over the interval [0, TI. Technically speaking, a cap is the sum of a number of basic contracts, known as caplets, which are defined as follows: 

The interval [0, TI is subdivided by the equidistant points 

$$
0 = T _ {0}, T _ {1}, \dots , T _ {n} = T.
$$

We use the notation 6 for the length of an elementary interval, i.e $\delta = T _ { i } - T _ { i - 1 }$ Typically, 6 is a quarter of a year, or half a year. 

The cap is working on some principal amount of money, denoted by K, and the cap rate is denoted by R. 

The floating rate of interest underlying the cap is not the short rate r, but rather some market rate, and we will assume that over the interval $[ T _ { i - 1 } , T _ { i } ]$ it is the LIBOR spot rate $\pmb { L } ( T _ { i - 1 } , T _ { i } )$ (see Section 20.2). 

Caplet i is now defined as the following contingent claim, paid at Ti, 

$$
\mathcal {X} _ {i} = K \delta \max [ L (T _ {i - 1}, T _ {i}) - R, 0 ].\tag{24.62}
$$

We now turn to the problem of pricing the caplet, and without loss of generality we may assume that $\mathbf K = \mathbf 1$ . We will also use the notation ${ \pmb x } ^ { + } = \operatorname* { m a x } [ { \pmb x } , { \pmb 0 } ]$ , so the caplet can be written as 

$$
\mathcal {X} = \delta (L - R) ^ {+},
$$

where $\mathrm { L } = L ( T _ { i - 1 } , T _ { i } )$ Denoting $p ( T _ { i - 1 } , T _ { i } )$ by p, and recalling that 

$$
L = \frac {1 - p}{p \delta},
$$

we have 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} \mathcal {X} & = \delta (L - R) ^ {+} = \delta (L - R) ^ {+} = \delta \left(\frac {1 - p}{p \delta} - R\right) ^ {+} \\ & = \left(\frac {1}{p} - (1 + \delta R)\right) ^ {+} = \left(\frac {1}{p} - R ^ {\star}\right) ^ {+} = \frac {R ^ {\star}}{p} \left(\frac {1}{R ^ {\star}} - p\right) ^ {+}, \end{array}
$$

where $\mathrm { R ^ { * } } = 1 + \delta R$ . It is, however, easily seen (why?) that a payment of $( R ^ { \star } / p ) \left( ( 1 / R ^ { \star } ) - p \right) ^ { + }$ a t time $\mathbf { \mathcal { T } } _ { i }$ is equivalent to a payment of $\mathbf { R } ^ { * } ( ( \dot { 1 } / \dot { R } ^ { \star } ) - p ) ^ { + }$ at time $T _ { i - 1 }$ 

Consequently we see that a caplet is equivalent to $\mathbf { R } ^ { * }$ put options on an underlying $\mathrm { T _ { i } } { \mathrm { - } } { \mathrm { b o n d } } ,$ where the exercise date of the option is at $T _ { i - 1 }$ and the exercise price is $1 / R ^ { \star }$ . An entire cap contract can thus be viewed as a portfolio of put options, and we may use the earlier results of the chapter to compute the theoretical price. 

A different approach to the pricing of caplets (and hence of caps) is to view the caplet claim in (24.62) as a formal option directly on the LIBOR rate, and noting that the LIBOR forward rate $L ( t ; T _ { i } , T _ { i + 1 } )$ is a martingale under $Q ^ { T _ { i + 1 } }$ This approach will be investigated in some detail in the chapter on LIBOR market models below.
