## 24.10 Notes

The first usage of a numeraire different from the risk free asset B was probably in Merton (1973), where however the technique is not explicitly discussed. The first to explicitly use a change of numeraire change was Margrabe (1978), who (referring to a discussion with S. Ross) used an underlying stock as numeraire in order to value an exchange option. The numeraire change is also used in Harrison and Kreps (1979), Harrison and Pliska (1981) and basically in all later 

![image](https://cdn-mineru.openxlab.org.cn/result/2026-11-17/ec4b01e7-219e-4b27-ae7f-89d97615f591/e81854a7962cf8b99303f37682b2dcf6a49121cc77d2521158accf3921a41d87.jpg)



works on the existence of martingale measures in order to reduce (as we did in Chapter 10) the general case to the basic case of zero short rate. In these papers, the numeraire change as such is however not put to systematic use as an instrument for facilitating the computation of option prices in complicated models. In the context of interest rate theory, changes of numeraire were then used and discussed independently by Geman (1989) and (in a Gaussian framework) Jamshidian (1989), who both used a bond maturing at a fixed time T as numeraire. A systematic study of general changes of numeraire has been carried out by Geman, El Karoui and h c h e t in a series of papers, and many of the results above can be found in Geman et al. (1995). For further examples of the change of numeraire technique, see Benninga et al. (2002).


# LIBOR AND SWAP MARKET MODELS

In the previous chapters we have concentrated on studying interest rate models based on infinitesimal interest rates like the instantaneous short rate and the instantaneous forward rates. While these objects are nice to handle from a mathematical point of view, they have two main disadvantages: 

The instantaneous short and forward rates can never be observed in real life. 

If you would like to calibrate your model to c a p or swaption data, then this is typically very complicated from a numerical point of view if you use one of the "instantaneous" models. 

A further fact from real life, which has been somewhat disturbing from a theoretical point of view is the following: 

For a very long time, the market practice has been to value caps, floors, and swaptions by using a formal extension of the Black (1976) model. Such an extension is typically obtained by an approximation argument where the short rate at one point in the argument is assumed to be determinstic, while later on in the argument the LIBOR rate is assumed to be stochastic. This is of course logically inconsistent. 

Despite this, the market happily continues to use Black-76 for the pricing of caps, floors, and swaptions. 

In a situation like this, where market practice seems to be at odds with academic work there are two possible attitudes for the theorist: you can join them (the market) or you can try to beat them, and since the fixed income market does not seem to collapse because of the use of Black-76, the more realistic alternative seems to be to join them. 

Thus there has appeared a natural demand for constructing logically consistent (and arbitrage free!) models having the property that the theoretical prices for caps, floors and swaptions produced by the model are of the Black-76 form. This project has in fact been carried out very successfully, starting with Miltersen et al. (1997), Brace et al, (1997) and Jamshidian (1998). The basic structure of the models is as follows: 

In stead of modeling instantaneous interest rates, we model discrete market rates like LIBOR rates in the LIBOR market models, or forward swap rates in the swap market models. 

Under a suitable choice of numeraire(s), these market rates can in fact be modeled log normally. 

# CAPS: DEFINITION AND MARKET PRACTICE

The market models will thus produce pricing formulas for caps and fioors (the LIBOR models), and swaptions (the swap market models) which are of the Black-76 type and thus conforming with market practice. 

By construction the market models are thus very easy to calibrate to market data for caps/floors and swaptions respectively. They are then used to price more exotic products. For this later pricing part, however, we will typically have to resort to some numerical method, like Monte Carlo. 

## 25.1 Caps: Definition and Market Practice

In this section we discuss LIBOR caps and the market practice for pricing and quoting these intruments. To this end we consider a fixed set of increasing maturities $T _ { 0 } , T _ { 1 } , \dots , T _ { N }$ and we define $\alpha _ { i }$ , by 

$$
\alpha_ {i} = T _ {i} - T _ {i - 1}, \quad i = 1, \dots , N.
$$

The number $\alpha _ { i }$ is known as the tenor, and in a typical application we could for example have all $\alpha _ { i }$ equal to a quarter of a year. 

Definition 25.1 W e let $p _ { i } ( t )$ denote the zero coupon bond price ${ \pmb p } ( t , T _ { i } )$ and let $L _ { i } ( t )$ ) denote the LIBOR forward rate (see Section 20.2), contracted at t, for the period $[ T _ { i - 1 } , T _ { i } ]$ , 2.e. 

$$
L _ {i} (t) = \frac {1}{\alpha_ {i}} \cdot \frac {p _ {i - 1} (t) - p _ {i} (t)}{p _ {i} (t)}, \quad i = 1, \dots , N.\tag{25.1}
$$

We recall that a cap with cap rate R and resettlement dates $T _ { 0 } , \ldots , T _ { N }$ is a contract which at time $T _ { i }$ gives the holder of the cap the amount 

$$
X _ {i} = \alpha_ {i} \cdot \max \left[ L _ {i} (T _ {i - 1}) - R, 0 \right],\tag{25.2}
$$

for each $i { = } 1 , \ldots , \ N$ . The cap is thus a portfolio of the individual caplets $X _ { 1 } , \ldots , X _ { N }$ . We note that the forward rate $L _ { i } ( T _ { i - 1 } )$ above is in fact the spot rate at time $\mathbf { \Delta } T _ { i - 1 }$ for the period $[ T _ { i - 1 } , T _ { i } ]$ ], and determined already at time $T _ { i - 1 }$ The amount Xi is thus determined at $\pmb { T _ { i - 1 } }$ but not payed out until at time Ti. We also note that, formally speaking, the caplet $X _ { i }$ i is a call option on the underlying spot rate. 

The market practice is to use the Black-76 formula for the pricing of caplets. 

Definition 25.2 (Black's Formula for Caplets) The Black-76 formula for the caplet 

$$
X _ {i} = \alpha_ {i} \cdot \max [ L (T _ {i - 1}, T _ {i}) - R, 0 ],\tag{25.3}
$$

is given by the expression 

$$
\mathbf {C a p l} _ {\mathbf {i}} ^ {\mathbf {B}} (t) = \alpha_ {i} \cdot p _ {i} (t) \left\{L _ {i} (t) N [ d _ {1} ] - R N [ d _ {2} ] \right\}, \quad i = 1, \dots , N,\tag{25.4}
$$

where 

$$
\begin{array}{l} d _ {1} = \frac {1}{\sigma_ {i} \sqrt {T _ {i} - t}} \left[ \ln \left(\frac {L _ {i} (t)}{R}\right) + \frac {1}{2} \sigma_ {i} ^ {2} (T - t) \right], \\ d _ {2} = d _ {1} - \sigma_ {i} \sqrt {T _ {i} - t}. \end{array}\tag{25.5}
$$

(25.6) 

The constant $\sigma _ { i }$ is known as the B l a c k volatility for caplet No. i. In order to make the dependence o n the Black volatility $\sigma _ { i }$ explicit we will sometimes write the caplet price as $C a p l _ { i } ^ { B } ( t ; \mathrm { a } , )$ 

It is implicit in the Black formula that the forward rates are lognormal (under some probability measure), but until recently there was no firm theoretical base for the use of the Black-76 formula for caplets. One of the main goals of this chapter is precisely that of investigating whether it is possible to build an arbitrage free model object which produces formulas of the Black type for caplet prices. 

In the market, cap prices are not quoted in monetary terms but instead in terms of i mp l i e d Black volatilities, and these volatilities can furthermore be quoted as flat volatilities or as sp o t volatilities (also known as forward volatilities) . They are defined as follows. 

Let us consider a fixed date t, the fixed set of dates $T _ { 0 } , T _ { 1 } , \dots , T _ { N }$ where $t \leq T _ { 0 } .$ , and a fixed cap rate R. We assume that, for each $i = 1 , \ldots , \mathrm { N }$ , there is a traded cap with resettlement dates $T _ { 0 } , T _ { 1 } , \dots , T _ { i } ,$ , and we denote the corresponding observed market price by $\mathbf { C a p _ { i } ^ { m } }$ . From this data we can easily compute the market prices for the corresponding caplets as 

$$
\operatorname{Capl} _ {\mathbf {i}} ^ {\mathbf {m}} (t) = \operatorname{Cap} _ {\mathbf {i}} ^ {\mathbf {m}} (t) - \operatorname{Cap} _ {\mathbf {i} - 1} ^ {\mathbf {m}} (t), \quad i = 1, \dots , N,\tag{25.7}
$$

with the convention $\mathbf { C a p _ { 0 } ^ { m } } ( t ) = 0$ . Alternatively, given market data for caplets we can easily compute the corresponding market data for caps. 

D efi n i ti o n 25.3 Given market price data as above, the implied Black volatilities are defined as follows. 

Th e implied fl a t v o l a ti l i ti e s $\bar { \sigma } _ { 1 } , \dots , \bar { \sigma } _ { N }$ are defined as the solutions of the equations 

$$
\operatorname{Cap} _ {\mathbf {i}} ^ {\mathbf {m}} (t) = \sum_ {\mathrm{k} = 1} ^ {i} \operatorname{Capl} _ {\mathbf {k}} ^ {\mathbf {B}} (t; \bar {\sigma} _ {i}), \quad i = 1, \dots , N.\tag{25.8}
$$

The implied forward or sp o t volatilities $\bar { \sigma } _ { 1 } , \dots , \bar { \sigma } _ { N }$ are defined as solution.~ of the equations 

$$
\mathbf {C a p l} _ {\mathbf {i}} ^ {\mathbf {m}} (t) = \mathbf {C a p l} _ {\mathbf {i}} ^ {\mathbf {B}} (t; \bar {\sigma} _ {i}), \quad i = 1, \dots , N.\tag{25.9}
$$

A sequence of implied volatilities $\bar { \sigma } _ { 1 } , \dots , \bar { \sigma } _ { N }$ ~ (Bat or spot) is called a volatility t e r m s tru c tu re . Note that we use the same notation $\bar { \sigma } _ { i }$ for flat as well as for spot volatilities. In applications this will be made clear by the context. 

Summarizing the formal definition above, the flat volatility $\bar { \sigma } _ { i }$ is volatility implied by the Black formula if you use the same volatility for each caplet in the cap with maturity $\mathbf { \delta } T _ { i }$ . The spot volatility $\sigma _ { i }$ is just the implied volatility from caplet No. i. The difference between flat and forward volatilities is thus similar to the difference between yields and forward rates. A typical shape of the volatility term structure (flat or spot) for caps with, say, a three months tenor is that it has an upward hump for maturities around two-three years, but that the long end of the curve is downward sloping. 

## 25.2 T h e LIBOR Market Model

We now turn from market practice to the construction of the so called LIBOR market models. To motivate these models let us consider the theoretical arbitrage free pricing of caps. The price $c _ { i } ( t )$ of a caplet No. i is of course on the one hand given by the standard risk neutral valuation formula 

$$
\mathbf {C a p l} _ {\mathbf {i}} (t) = \alpha_ {i} E ^ {Q} \left[ \mathrm{e} ^ {- \int_ {0} ^ {T _ {i}} r (s) \mathrm{d} s}. \max \left[ L _ {i} (T _ {i - 1}) - R, 0 \right] \mid \mathcal {F} _ {t} \right], \quad i = 1, \dots , N,
$$

but it is much more natural to use the $\mathbf { \delta } T _ { i }$ forward measure to obtain 

$$
\operatorname{Capl} _ {\mathbf {i}} (t) = \alpha_ {i} p _ {i} (t) E ^ {T _ {i}} \left[ \max \left[ L _ {i} \left(T _ {i - 1}\right) - R, 0 \right] \mid \mathcal {F} _ {t} \right], \quad i = 1 \dots , N,\tag{25.10}
$$

where $E ^ { T _ { i } }$ denotes expectation under the $Q ^ { T _ { i } }$ . In order to have a more compact notation we will from now on denote $Q ^ { T _ { i } }$ 9 y $\mathbf { Q } ^ { \mathrm { i } }$ . 

The focal point of the LIBOR models is the following simple result. 

Lemma 25.4 For every $\pmb { i } = 1 , \ldots ,  { \mathrm { N } }$ , the LIBOR process $L _ { i }$ is a martingale under the comsponding fornard measure $Q ^ { T _ { i } }$ j, on the internal $[ 0 , T _ { i - 1 } ]$ 

Proof We have 

$$
\alpha_ {i} \cdot L _ {i} (t) = \frac {p _ {i - 1} (t)}{p _ {i} (t)} - 1.
$$

The process 1 is obviously a martingale under any measure. The process $\pmb { p _ { i - 1 } } / p _ { i }$ is the price of the $T _ { i - 1 }$ bond normalized by the numeraire $\pmb { p _ { i } }$ . Since $\pmb { p _ { i } }$ is the numeraire for the martingale measure $Q ^ { T _ { i } }$ i, the process ${ p _ { i - 1 } } / { p _ { i } }$ is thus trivially a martingale on the interval $[ 0 , T _ { i - 1 } ]$ . Thus $\mathbf { \alpha _ { \hat { \ell } } } \mathbf { \mathit { L } _ { i } }$ is a martingale and hence $L _ { i }$ is also a martingale. □ 

The basic idea is now to define the LIBOR rates such that, for each i, $L _ { i } ( T )$ will be lognormal under "its own" measure $Q ^ { 2 }$ , since then d l caplet prices in (25.10) will be given by a Black type formula. In order to do this we consider the following objects as given a priori 

A set of resettlement dates $T _ { 0 } , \dots , T _ { N }$ 

An arbitrage free market bond with maturities $T _ { 0 } , \ldots , T _ { N }$ 

A k-dimensional $Q ^ { N }$ - ~ i e n e rprocess $\mathbf { W } ^ { \mathbf { N } }$ 

For each $i = 1 , \ldots , \Nu$ a deterministic function of time $\sigma _ { i } ( t )$ 

An initial nonnegative forward rate term structure $L _ { 1 } ( 0 ) , \dots , L _ { N } ( 0 )$ 

For each $i = 1 , \ldots , \mathrm { N }$ , we define $\mathbf { W ^ { i } }$ as the k-dimensional Q<sup>i</sup>-Wiener process generated by $\mathbf { W } ^ { \mathrm { N } }$ under the Girsanov transformation $\mathrm { { Q } ^ { \bar { N } }  \mathrm { { Q } ^ { i } } }$ 

Definition 25.5 If the LIBOR forward rates have the dynamics 

$$
\mathrm{d} L _ {i} (t) = L _ {i} (t) \sigma_ {i} (t) \mathrm{d} W ^ {i} (\mathrm{t}), \quad i = 1, \dots , N,\tag{25.11}
$$

where W<sup>i</sup> is Q<sup>i</sup>- Wiener as described above, then we say that we have a discrete tenor LIBOR market model with volatilities $\sigma _ { 1 } , \ldots , \sigma _ { N }$ 

From the definition above it is not obvious that, given a specification of $\sigma _ { 1 } , \ldots , \sigma _ { N }$ , there exists a corresponding LIBOR market model. In order to arrive at the basic pricing formulas a quickly as possible we will temporarily ignore the existence problem, but we will come back to it below and thus provide the missing link. 

## 25.3 Pricing Caps in the LIBOR Model

Given a LIBOR market model, the pricing of a caplet, and hence also a cap, is trivial. Since $\mathbf { { { L } } } _ { i }$ in (25.11) is just a GBM we obtain 

$$
L _ {i} (T) = L _ {i} (t) \cdot \mathrm{e} ^ {\int_ {t} ^ {T} \sigma_ {i} (s) \mathrm{d} W ^ {i} (s) - \frac {1}{2} \int_ {t} ^ {T} \| \sigma_ {i} (s) \| ^ {2} \mathrm{d} s}.
$$

Since $\sigma _ { i }$ is assumed to be deterministic this implies that, conditional on $\mathcal { F } _ { t }$ t $\pmb { L } _ { i } ( T )$ is lognormal, i.e. we can write 

$$
L _ {i} (T) = L _ {i} (t) \mathrm{e} ^ {Y _ {i} (t, T)},
$$

where $Y _ { i } ( t , \mathrm { T } )$ is normally distributed with expected value 

$$
m _ {i} (t, T) = - \frac {1}{2} \int_ {t} ^ {T} \| \sigma_ {i} (s) \| ^ {2} d s,\tag{25.12}
$$

and variance 

$$
\Sigma_ {i} ^ {2} (t, T) = \int_ {t} ^ {T} \| \sigma_ {i} (s) \| ^ {2} d s.\tag{25.13}
$$

Using these results and (25.10), a simple calculation gives us the pricing formula for caps. Alternatively we see that the expectation ${ \bf E ^ { i } }$ for the cap price in (25.10) is just the call price, within the Black-Scholes framework, in a world with zero short rate on an underlying traded asset with lognormal distribution as above. 

Proposition 25.6 In the LIBOR market model, the caplet prices are given by 

$$
\operatorname{Capl} _ {\mathbf {i}} (t) = \alpha_ {i} \cdot p _ {i} (t) \left\{L _ {i} (t) N [ d _ {1} ] - R N [ d _ {2} ] \right\}, \quad i = 1, \dots , N,\tag{25.14}
$$

where 

$$
\begin{array}{l} d _ {1} = \frac {1}{\Sigma_ {i} (t , T _ {i - 1})} \left[ \ln \left(\frac {L _ {i} (t)}{R}\right) + \frac {1}{2} \Sigma_ {i} ^ {2} (t, T _ {i - 1}) \right], \\ d _ {2} = d _ {1} - \Sigma_ {i} (t, T _ {i - 1}), \end{array}\tag{25.15}
$$

(25.16) 

with $\Sigma _ { i }$ defined by (25.13). 

We thus see that each caplet price is given by a Black type formula. 

Remark 25.3.1 Sometimes it is more convenient working with a LIBOR model of the form 

$$
\mathrm{d} L _ {i} (t) = L _ {i} (t) \sigma_ {i} (t) \mathrm{d} W ^ {i} (t), \quad i = 1, \dots , N,\tag{25.17}
$$

where $\sigma _ { i } ( t )$ is a scalar deterministic function, $\mathbf { W ^ { i } }$ is a scalar @-wiener process. Then the formulas above still hold if we replace $\| \sigma _ { i } \| ^ { 2 }$ by $\sigma _ { i } ^ { 2 }$ We can also allow for correlation betweep the various Wiener processes, but this will not affect the pricing of caps and floors. Such a correlation will however affect the pricing of more complicated products. 

## 25.4 Terminal Measure Dynamics and Existence

We now turn to the question whether there always exists a LIBOR market model for any given specification of the deterministic volatilities $\sigma _ { 1 } , \ldots , \sigma _ { N }$ . In order to even get started we first have to specify all LIBOR rates $\ L _ { 1 } , \ldots , L _ { N }$ under one common measure, and the canonical choice is the terminal measure $\mathrm { Q } ^ { \mathrm { N } }$ 

Our problem is then basically that of carrying out a two stage program: 

Specify all LIBOR rates under $\boldsymbol { \mathrm { Q } } ^ { \mathrm { N } }$ with dynamics of the form 

$$
\mathrm{d} L _ {i} (t) = L _ {i} (t) \mu_ {i} (t, L (t)) \mathrm{d} t + L _ {i} (t) \sigma_ {i} (t) \mathrm{d} W ^ {N} (t), \quad i = 1, \dots , N,\tag{25.18}
$$

![image](https://cdn-mineru.openxlab.org.cn/result/2026-11-17/ec4b01e7-219e-4b27-ae7f-89d97615f591/f8ab27b788ea52a23973ec207565494d2d354bec66c90ba0380aeeda9d250c11.jpg)


where $L ( t ) = [ L _ { 1 } ( \mathrm { t } ) , \ldots , L _ { N } ( t ) ] ^ { \star }$ *, and $\mu _ { i }$ is some deterministic function. 

Show that, for some suitable choice of $\mu _ { 1 } , \ldots , \mu _ { N }$ ~ ,the $\boldsymbol { \mathrm { Q } } ^ { \mathrm { N } }$ dynamics in (25.18) will imply $Q ^ { \imath }$ dynamics of the form (25.11). 

In order to carry out this program we need to see how $W ^ { N }$ is transformed into $\mathbf { W } ^ { \mathbf { i } }$ as we change measure from $\mathrm { Q } ^ { \mathrm { N } }$ to $\mathbf { Q ^ { i } }$ . We do this inductively by studying the effect of the Girsanov transformation from $Q ^ { \imath }$ to $Q ^ { i - 1 }$ 

Remark 25.4.1 We have a small but irritating notational problem. LIBOR rates are typically denoted by the letter $^ { 6 6 } \mathrm { \mathbf { L } } ^ { 9 }$ , but this is also a standard notation for a likelihood process. In order to avoid confusion we therefore introduce the notational convention that, in this chapter only, likelihood processes will be denoted by the letter $\eta .$ . In particular we introduce the notation 

$$
\eta_ {i} ^ {j} (t) = \frac {\mathrm{d} Q ^ {j}}{\mathrm{d} Q ^ {i}}, \text { on } \mathcal {F} _ {t} \quad \text { for } i, j = 1, \dots , N\tag{25.19}
$$

In order to get some idea of how we should choose the $Q ^ { N }$ drifts of the LIBOR rates in (25.18) we will now perform some informal calculations. We thus (informally) assume that the LIBOR dynamics are of the form (25.18) under $Q ^ { \pmb { N } }$ and that they are also of the form (25.11) under their own martingale measure. From Proposition 24.4 we know that the Radon-Nikodym derivative $\eta _ { i } ^ { j }$ is given by 

$$
\eta_ {i} ^ {j} (t) = \frac {p _ {i} (0)}{p _ {j} (0)} \cdot \frac {p _ {j} (t)}{p _ {i} (t)},\tag{25.20}
$$

and in particular 

$$
\eta_ {i} ^ {i - 1} (t) = a _ {i} \cdot \frac {p _ {i - 1} (t)}{p _ {i} (t)} = a _ {i} \left(1 + \alpha_ {i} L _ {i} (t)\right),\tag{25.21}
$$

where $a _ { i } = p _ { i } ( 0 ) / p _ { i - 1 } ( 0 )$ From this formula we can now easily compute the $\eta _ { i } ^ { i - 1 }$ dynamics under $Q ^ { \imath }$ as 

$$
\mathrm{d} \eta_ {i} ^ {i - 1} (t) = a _ {i} \alpha_ {i} \mathrm{d} L _ {i} (t).\tag{25.22}
$$

Assuming (still informally) that the $L _ { i } – \mathbf { d y n a m i c s }$ are as in (25.11), and using (25.1) we then obtain 

$$
\mathrm{d} \eta_ {i} ^ {i - 1} (t) = a _ {i} \alpha_ {i} L _ {i} (t) \sigma_ {i} (t) \mathrm{d} W ^ {i} (t)
$$

$$
= a _ {i} \alpha_ {i} \frac {1}{\alpha_ {i}} \left(\frac {p _ {i - 1} (t)}{p _ {i} (t)} - 1\right) \sigma_ {i} (t) \mathrm{d} W ^ {i} (t)\tag{25.23}
$$

$$
= \eta_ {i} ^ {i - 1} (t) a _ {i} \alpha_ {i} \frac {1}{\eta_ {i} ^ {i - 1} (t)} \left(\frac {p _ {i - 1} (t)}{p _ {i} (t)} - 1 \right. \sigma_ {i} (t) d W ^ {i} (t).\tag{25.24}
$$

(25.25) 

Using (25.21) we finally obtain 

$$
\mathrm{d} \eta_ {i} ^ {i - 1} (t) = \eta_ {i} ^ {i - 1} (t) \frac {\alpha_ {i} L _ {i} (t)}{1 + \alpha_ {\mathrm{a} _ {2}}} \sigma_ {i} (\mathrm{t}) \mathrm{d} W ^ {i} (\mathrm{t}).\tag{25.26}
$$

Thus, the Girsanov kernel for $\eta _ { i } ^ { i - 1 }$ is given by 

$$
\frac {\alpha_ {i} L _ {i} (t)}{1 + \alpha_ {i} L _ {i} (t)} \sigma_ {i} ^ {\star} (t),\tag{25.27}
$$

so from the Girsanov Theorem, we have the relation 

$$
\mathrm{d} W ^ {i} (t) = \frac {\alpha_ {i} L _ {i} (t)}{1 + \alpha_ {i} L _ {i} (t)} \sigma_ {i} ^ {*} (t) \mathrm{dt} + \mathrm{d} W ^ {i - 1} (t).\tag{25.28}
$$

Applying this inductively we obtain 

$$
\mathrm{d} W ^ {i} (t) = - \sum_ {k = i + 1} ^ {N} \frac {\alpha_ {k} L _ {k} (t)}{1 + \alpha_ {k} L _ {k} (t)} \sigma_ {k} ^ {\star} (t) \mathrm{d} t + \mathrm{d} W ^ {N} (t),\tag{25.29}
$$

and plugging this into (25.11) we can finally obtain the $\mathrm { Q } ^ { \mathrm { N } }$ dynamics of $\mathbf { { { L } } _ { i } }$ (see (25.30)). 

All this was done under the informal assumption that there actually existed a LIBOR model satisfying both (25.11) and (25.18). We can however easily turn the argument around and we have the following existence result. 

Proposition 25.7 Consider a given volatility structure $\sigma _ { 1 } , \sigma _ { N }$ ~ , where each a, is assumed to be bounded, a probability measure $\mathrm { Q } ^ { \mathrm { N } }$ and a standard $\mathrm { Q } ^ { \mathrm { N } }$ - Wiener process $\mathbf { W } ^ { \mathbf { N } }$ . Define the processes $L _ { 1 } , \ldots , L _ { N }$ by 

$$
\mathrm{d} L _ {i} (t) = - L _ {i} (t) \left(\sum_ {k = i + 1} ^ {N} \overline {{{1 + \alpha_ {k} L _ {k} (t)}}} \sigma_ {k} (t) \sigma_ {i} ^ {\star} (t)\right) \mathrm{d} t + L _ {i} (t) \sigma_ {i} (t) \mathrm{d} W ^ {N} (t),\tag{25.30}
$$

for $\mathbf { i } = 1 , \ldots , \mathbf { N }$ where we use the convention $\Sigma _ { N } ^ { N } ( \dots ) { = } 0$ . Then the $Q ^ { 2 } - d y n a m i c s$ of $L _ { i }$ are given by (25.11). Thus there exists a LIBOR model with the given volatility structure. 

Proof Given that (25.30) has a solution for $\mathbf { i } = 1 , \ldots , \mathbf { N }$ , and that the Girsanov kernel in (25.27) satisfies the Novikov condition, the proof consists of exactly the calculations above. As for the existence of a solution of (25.30), this is trivial for $i = \Nu$ since then the equation reads 

$$
\mathrm{d} L _ {N} (t) = L _ {i} (t) \sigma_ {N} (t) \mathrm{d} W ^ {N} (t),
$$

which is just GBM and since $\sigma _ { N }$ is bounded a solution does exist. Assume now that (25.30) admits a solution for $\mathrm { k = i + 1 , \ldots , N }$ . We can then write the ith component of (25.30) as 

$$
\mathrm{d} L _ {i} (t) = L _ {i} (t) \mu_ {i} [ t, L _ {i + 1} (t), \dots , L _ {N} (t) ] \mathrm{d} t + L _ {i} (T) \sigma_ {i} (t) \mathrm{d} W ^ {N} (t),
$$

where the point is that $\mu _ { i }$ does only depend on $L _ { k }$ for $\mathrm { k } = \mathrm { i } + 1 , \ldots , \mathrm { N }$ and not on $L _ { i }$ . Denoting the vector $( L _ { i + 1 } , \ldots , L _ { N } )$ by $L _ { i + 1 } ^ { N }$ we thus have the explicit solution 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & {L _ {i} (t) = L _ {i} (0) \exp \biggl \{\int_ {0} ^ {t} \biggl (\mu_ {i} \bigl [ s, L _ {i + 1} ^ {N} (s) \bigr ] - \frac {1}{2} \| \sigma_ {i} \| ^ {2} (s) \biggr) \mathrm{d} s \biggr \}} \\ & {\qquad \times \exp \biggl \{\int_ {0} ^ {t} \mu_ {i} \bigl [ s, L _ {i + 1} ^ {N} (s) \bigr ] \mathrm{d} W ^ {N} (s) \biggr \},} \end{array}
$$

thus proving existence by induction. It also follows by induction that, given an initial positive LIBOR term structure, all LIBOR rate processes will be positive. From this we see that the Girsanov kernel in (25.27) is also bounded and thus it satisifies the Novikov condition. □ 

Remark 25.4.2 Sometimes it is more convenient working with a LIBOR model of the form 

$$
\mathrm{d} L _ {i} (t) = L _ {i} (t) \sigma_ {i} (t) \mathrm{d} W _ {i} (\mathrm{t}), \quad \mathrm{i} = 1, \dots , \mathrm{N},\tag{25.31}
$$

where $\sigma _ { i } ( t )$ is a scalar deterministic function, $W _ { i }$ is a scalar $Q ^ { \imath } { - } \mathbf { W }$ iener process, and where we assume a given correlation structure $\mathrm { d } W _ { i } ( t ) \mathrm { d } W _ { j } ( t ) = \rho _ { i j }$ . This can easily be obtained by a small variation of the arguments above, and eqn (25.30) is then replaced by 

$$
\mathrm{d} L _ {i} (t) = - L _ {i} (t) \left(\sum_ {k = i + 1} ^ {N} \frac {\alpha_ {k} L _ {k} (t)}{1 + \alpha_ {k} L _ {k} (t)} \sigma_ {i} (t) \sigma_ {k} (t) \rho_ {i k}\right) \mathrm{d} t + L _ {i} (t) \sigma_ {i} (t) \mathrm{d} W _ {i} ^ {N} (t),\tag{25.32}
$$

where $W _ { i } ^ { N }$ is the $\mathrm { Q } ^ { \mathrm { N _ { - w } } }$ iener process generated by $W _ { i }$ under the Girsanov transformation $Q ^ { \imath } \to Q ^ { \Nu }$ 

## 25.5 Calibration and Simulation

Suppose that we want to price some exotic (i.e. not a cap or a floor) interest rate derivative, like a Bermudan swaption, performing this with a LIBOR model means that we typically carry out the following two steps: 

Use implied Black volatilities in order to calibrate the model parameters to market data. 

a Use Monte Carlo (or some other numerical method) to price the exotic instrument. 

In this section we mainly discuss the calibration part, and only comment briefly on the numerical aspects. For numerics and simulation see the Notes. 

Let us thus assume that, for the resettlement dates $T _ { 0 } , . . . , T _ { N }$ , we are given an empirical term structure of implied forward volatilities, $\bar { \sigma } _ { 1 } , \dots , \bar { \sigma } _ { N }$ i.e. the implied Black volatilities for all caplets. For simplicity we assume that we are standing at time $\mathbf { t } = 0$ . Comparing the Black formula (25.4) with (25.14) we see that in order to calibrate the model we have to choose the deterministic LIBOR volatilities $\sigma _ { 1 } ( \cdot ) , \ldots , \sigma _ { N } ( \cdot )$ , such that 

$$
\bar {\sigma} _ {i} = \frac {1}{T _ {i}} \int_ {0} ^ {T _ {i - 1}} \| \sigma_ {i} (s) \| ^ {2} d s, \quad i = 1, \dots , N.\tag{25.33}
$$

Alternatively, if we use a scalar Wiener process for each LIBOR rate we must choose the scalar function $\sigma _ { i } ( \cdot )$ such that 

$$
\bar {\sigma} _ {i} = \frac {1}{T _ {i}} \int_ {0} ^ {T _ {i - 1}} \sigma_ {i} ^ {2} (s) \mathrm{d} s, \quad i = 1, \dots , N.\tag{25.34}
$$

This is obviously a highly underdetermined system, so in applications it is common to make some structural assumption about the shape of the volatility functions. Below is a short and incomplete list of popular specifications. We use the formalism with a scalar Wiener process for each forward rate, and we recall that $\boldsymbol { L } _ { i }$ lives on the time interval $0 \leq t \leq T _ { i - 1 }$ We also introduce the temporary convention that $\begin{array} { r } { T _ { - 1 } = 0 . } \end{array}$ 

1. For each $\mathbf { i } = 1 , \ldots , \mathrm { N }$ , assume that the corresponding volatility is constant in time, i.e. that 

$$
\sigma_ {i} (t) = \sigma_ {i}
$$

for $0 \leq \mathfrak { t } \leq T _ { i - 1 }$ 

2. For each $\mathbf { i } = 1 , \ldots , \mathrm { N }$ , assume that $\sigma _ { i }$ is piecewise constant, i.e. that 

$$
\sigma_ {i} (t) = \sigma_ {i j}, \quad \text { for } T _ {j - 1} <   t \leq T _ {j}, \mathrm{j=0,...,i-1}.
$$

3. As in item 2, but with the requirement that the volatility only depends on the number of resettlement dates left to maturity, i.e. that 

$$
\sigma_ {i j} = \beta_ {i - j}, \quad \text { for } T _ {j - 1} <   t \leq T _ {j}, j = 0, \dots , i - 1,
$$

where $\beta _ { 1 } , \ldots , \beta _ { N }$ are fixed numbers. 

4. As in item 2, with the further specification that 

$$
\sigma^ {i j} = \beta i \gamma_ {j}, \quad \text { for } T _ {j - 1} <   t \leq T _ {j}, j = 0, \dots , i - 1,
$$

where $\beta _ { i }$ and $\gamma _ { j }$ are fked numbers. 

5. Assume some simple functional parameterized form of the volatilities such as for example 

$$
\sigma_ {i} (t) = q _ {i} (T _ {i - 1} - t) \mathrm{e} ^ {\beta_ {i} (T _ {i - 1} - t)}
$$

where $q _ { i } ( \cdot )$ ) is some polynomial and $\beta _ { i }$ is a real number. 

Assuming that the model has been calibrated to market data, Monte Carlo simulation is the standard tool for computing prices of exotics. Since the SDEs (25.30) and (25.32) are too complicated to allow analytical solutions, we have to resort to simulation of discretized versions of the equations. 

The simplest way to discretize (25.30) is to introduce a grid of length h and use the following recursive Euler scheme: 

$$
\begin{array}{l} L _ {i} ((n + 1) h) = L _ {i} (n h) - L _ {i} (n h) \left(\sum_ {k = i + 1} ^ {N} \frac {\alpha_ {k} L _ {k} (n h)}{1 + \alpha_ {k} L _ {k} (n h)} \sigma_ {i} (n h) \sigma_ {k} ^ {*} (n h)\right) h \\ + L _ {i} (n h) \sigma_ {i} (n h) \left\{W ^ {N} ((n + 1) h) - W ^ {N} (n h) \right\}. \end{array} \tag {25}\tag{25.35}
$$

However, from the point of view of numerical stability it is preferable to use a discretization of the SDE for ln $( L _ { i } )$ . Using It8 we easily obtain 

$$
\mathrm{d} \ln L _ {i} (t) = - \left(\frac {1}{2} \sigma_ {i} ^ {2} (t) + \sigma_ {i} (t) \sigma_ {k} ^ {\star} (t) \sum_ {k = i + 1} ^ {\mathrm{N}} \frac {\alpha_ {k} L _ {k} (t)}{1 - \alpha_ {k} L _ {k} (t)}\right) \mathrm{dt} + \sigma_ {i} (t) \mathrm{d} W ^ {N} (t).\tag{25.36}
$$

The point of this is that we now have a deterministic diffusion part, which leads to improved convergence of the corresponding discrete scheme 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \ln L _ {i} ((n + 1) h) = \ln L _ {i} (n h) - \mathrm{h} \left(\frac {1}{2} \sigma_ {i} ^ {2} (\mathrm{n} h) + \sum_ {k = i + 1} ^ {\mathrm{N}} \frac {\alpha_ {k} L _ {k} (n h)}{1 + \alpha_ {k} L _ {k} (n h)} \sigma_ {i} (n h) \sigma_ {k} ^ {\star} (n h)\right) \\ + \sigma_ {i} (n h) \left\{W ^ {N} ((n + 1) h) - W ^ {N} (n h) \right\}. \end{array} \tag {25.37}
$$

## 25.6 The Discrete Savings Account

In the LIBOR models discussed above there exists a forward neutral martingale measure $Q ^ { 2 } = Q ^ { T _ { i } }$ * for each $i = 1 , \ldots , \Nu$ , but so far we have not seen any risk neutral measure $\mathbf { Q ^ { B } }$ for the bank account B, (also known as the savings account) and in fact we have not even seen a bank account process in the model. A natural question is therefore to investigate whether the LIBOR model will automatically imply a money account process B, as well as a corresponding risk neutral measure $Q ^ { \hat { B } }$ 

In this context it is, however, not quite clear what one would mean by a bank account. Since we are working in continuous time, one possibility is to look for a continuous bank account of the form we have seen earlier in the book, i.e. one with dynamics 

$$
\mathrm{d} B (t) = r (t) B (t) \mathrm{dt},
$$

where r is the continuously compounded short rate. However, since we have modeled discrete forward rates it would be unnatural to mix those with a continuously compounded short rate, so the natural choice would be to look for a bank account which is resettled at the points $T _ { 0 } , \dots , T _ { N }$ 

In order to construct the bank account we recall that the essential property is that it should be riskless on a local time scale, i.e. riskless between $T _ { n }$ and $\scriptstyle { T _ { N } }$ for each n. The obvious way to achieve this is by forming the discretely rebalanced self financing portfolio specified by constantly rolling over the bond of the shortest remaining maturity. More formally, suppose that we are standing at $T _ { 0 }$ and consider the following portfolio strategy: 

1. At $\pmb { T _ { 0 } }$ invest one unit of money into the $\pmb { T _ { 1 } }$ bond. 

2. At $T _ { 1 }$ sell the $\pmb { T _ { 1 } }$ bond and invest everything in the $\pmb { T _ { 2 } }$ bond. 

3. Repeat this procedure recursively until $\scriptstyle { T _ { N } }$ . 

Denoting the value of this self financing portfolio by B we immediately have 

$$
B (T _ {N}) = \frac {B (T _ {n})}{p (T _ {n} , T _ {N})}, \quad n = 0, \dots , N - 1,\tag{25.38}
$$

and using the relation $p ( T _ { n } , T _ { N } ) = [ 1 + \alpha _ { N } L ( T _ { n } , T _ { N } ) ] ^ { - 1 }$ we obtain the discrete B dynamics as 

(25.39) 

$$
B (T _ {N}) = \left(1 + \alpha_ {N} L (T _ {n}, T _ {N})\right) B (T _ {n}),\tag{25.40}
$$

or, more explicitly 

$$
B (T _ {n}) = \prod_ {\mathrm{k} = 0} ^ {n - 1} \frac {1}{p (T _ {k} , T _ {k + 1})},\tag{25.41}
$$

alternatively, 

$$
B (T _ {n}) = \prod_ {k = 0} ^ {n - 1} [ 1 + \alpha_ {k + 1} L (T _ {k}, T _ {k + 1}) ].\tag{25.42}
$$

We note that B is indeed locally risk free in the sense that $B ( T _ { N } )$ ) is known already at time $T _ { n }$ , i.e. as a discrete time process B is predictable in the sense of Appendix C. 

We can now easily determine the martingle measure corresponding to the discrete saving account. 

Proposition 25.8 The Radon-Nikodym derivative for the change from $\mathrm { Q } ^ { \mathrm { N } }$ to $\mathrm { Q } ^ { \mathrm { B } }$ is given by 

$$
\frac {\mathrm{d} Q ^ {B}}{\mathrm{d} Q ^ {N}} = p (0, T _ {N}) B (T _ {N}), o n \mathcal {F} _ {T _ {N}}\tag{25.43}
$$

Proof From Proposition 24.4 we have (on $\mathcal { F } _ { T _ { N } } )$ 

$$
\frac {\mathrm{d} Q ^ {B}}{\mathrm{d} Q ^ {N}} \stackrel {.} {=} \frac {B (T _ {N})}{p (T _ {N} , T _ {N})} \cdot \frac {B (0)}{p (0 , T _ {N})},
$$

and since $P ( T _ { N } , T _ { N } ) = 1$ and $B ( { \bf 0 } ) = { \bf 1 }$ we have the result. 

## 25.7 Swaps

We now move from the LIBOR Market Models to the the Swap Market Models. Consider a fixed set of resettlement dates $T _ { 0 } , T _ { 1 } , \dots , T _ { N }$ , with the usual notation $\alpha _ { i } = T _ { i } - T _ { i - 1 }$ . From Section 20.3.3 we recall that in an interest rate swap, a set of floating rate payments (the jloaiing leg) are exchanged for a set of fixed payments (the fixed leg). The terminology for swaps always refers to the fixed leg, so the holder of a reciever swap with tenor $T _ { N } - T _ { n }$ will, at the dates $T _ { n + 1 } , \dots , T _ { N }$ , receive the fixed leg and pay the floating leg. For a payer swap the payments go in the other direction. For short we will refer to this swap as a $T _ { n } \mathrm { ~ x ~ } ( T _ { N } - T _ { n } )$ ) swap. We now make this precise. 

Definition 25.9 The payments i n a $T _ { n } \ d \chi \left( T _ { N } - T _ { n } \right)$ payer swap are as follows: 

Payments will be made and received a $T _ { n + 1 } , T _ { n + 2 } , \ldots , T _ { N } ,$ 

a For every elementary period $[ T _ { i } , T _ { i + 1 } ] , i = n , \dots , N - I$ , the LIBOR rate $L _ { i + 1 } ( T _ { i } )$ ) is set at time $T _ { i }$ and the floating leg 

$$
\alpha_ {i + 1} \cdot L _ {i + 1} (T _ {i}),\tag{25.44}
$$

is received at $T _ { i + 1 }$ 

a For the same period the jixed leg 

$$
\alpha_ {i + 1}. K\tag{25.45}
$$

is payed at $T _ { i + 1 }$ 

It is easy to see (exercise for the reader) that the arbitrage free value, at $t < T _ { n }$ , of the floating payment made at $\mathbf { \delta } _ { T _ { i } }$ is given by 

$$
p (t, T _ {i}) - p (t, T _ {i + 1}),
$$

so the total value of the floating side at time t for $t \leq { \pmb T } _ { \pmb { n } }$ equals 

$$
\sum_ {i = n} ^ {N - 1} \left[ p (t, T _ {i}) - p (t, T _ {i + 1}) \right] = p _ {n} (t) - p _ {N} (t).
$$

The total value at time t of the fixed side equals 

$$
\sum_ {i = n} ^ {N - 1} p (t, T _ {i + 1}) \alpha_ {i + 1} K = K \sum_ {i = n + 1} ^ {N} \alpha_ {i} p _ {i} (t),
$$

so the net value $\mathbf { P S _ { n } ^ { N } } ( t ; K )$ of the $T _ { n } \mathrm { ~ X ~ } ( T _ { N } - T _ { n } )$ ) payer swap at time $t < T _ { n }$ is thus given by 

$$
\mathbf {P S} _ {\mathbf {n}} ^ {\mathbf {N}} (t; K) = p _ {n} (t) - p _ {N} (t) - K \sum_ {i = n + 1} ^ {N} \alpha_ {i} p _ {i} (t).\tag{25.46}
$$

From Section 20.3.3 we recall the following definition. 

Definition 25.10 The par or forward swap rate $R _ { n } ^ { N } ( t )$ t ) of the $T _ { n } \times \left( T _ { N } - T _ { n } \right)$ swap is the value of K for which $\mathbf { P S _ { n } ^ { N } } ( t ; K ) { \bar { = } } 0 $ , i.e. 

$$
R _ {n} ^ {N} (t) = \frac {p _ {n} (t) - p _ {N} (t)}{\sum_ {i = n + 1} ^ {N} \alpha_ {i} p _ {i} (t)}.\tag{25.47}
$$

The first crucial observation to make at this point is that in the formula for the par swap rate we can interpret the denominator $\textstyle \sum _ { i = n + 1 } ^ { N } \alpha _ { i } p _ { i } ( t )$ as the value, at t of a traded asset, namely as a buy-and-hold portfolio consisting, for each i, of $\alpha _ { i }$ units of the zero coupon bond maturing at $\pmb { T _ { i } }$ i. This object is so important that we give it a separate name. 

Definition 25.11 For each pair n, k with $\mathbf { n } < \mathbf { k }$ , the process $S _ { n } ^ { k } ( t )$ is defined by 

$$
S _ {n} ^ {k} (t) = \sum_ {i = n + 1} ^ {k} \alpha_ {i} p (t, T _ {i}).\tag{25.48}
$$

$S _ { n } ^ { k }$ is referred to as the accrual factor or as t h e present value of a basis point. 

With this terminology we can express the par swap rate as 

$$
R _ {n} ^ {N} (t) = \frac {p _ {n} (t) - p _ {N} (t)}{S _ {n} ^ {N} (t)}, \quad 0 \leq t \leq T _ {n}.\tag{25.49}
$$

In the market there are no quoted prices for different swaps. Instead there are market quotes for the par swap rates $R _ { n } ^ { N }$ , and we see that from these we can easily compute the arbitrage free price for a payer swap with swap rate K by the formula 

$$
\mathbf {P S} _ {\mathbf {n}} ^ {\mathbf {N}} (\mathrm{t}; \mathrm{K}) = \big (R _ {n} ^ {N} (t) - \mathrm{K} \big) S _ {n} ^ {N} (\mathrm{t}).\tag{25.50}
$$

## 25.8 Swaptions: Definition a n d Market Practice

The definition of a swaption (short for "swap option") is as follows. 

Definition 25.12 A $T _ { n } \mathrm { ~ x ~ } ( T _ { N } - T _ { n } )$ payer swaption with swaption strike K is a contract which at the exercise date $T _ { n }$ gives the holder the right but not the obligation to enter into a $T _ { n } \times \left( T _ { N } - T _ { n } \right)$ swap with the fied swap rate K . 

We thus see that the payer swaption is a contingent $\scriptstyle { { \mathcal { T } } _ { n } }$ -claim $X _ { n } ^ { N }$ defined by 

$$
X _ {n} ^ {N} = \max \left[ \mathbf {P S} _ {n} ^ {N} (T _ {n}; \mathrm{K}); 0 \right],\tag{25.51}
$$

which, using (25.49), we can write as 

$$
X _ {n} ^ {N} = \max \left[ R _ {n} ^ {N} (T _ {n}) - \mathrm{K}; 0 \right] S _ {n} ^ {N} (T _ {n}).\tag{25.52}
$$

Expressed in the numeraire $S _ { n } ^ { N }$ , the swaption is thus formally a call option on $R _ { n } ^ { \tilde { N } }$ with strike price K . The market practice is to compute swaption prices by using a formal extension of the Black-76 formula and to quote prices in terms of the implied Black volatilities. 

Definition 25.13 (Black's Formula for Swaptions) The Black-76 formula for a $T _ { n } \mathrm { ~ } x \left( T _ { N } - T , \right)$ payer swaption with strike K is defined as 

$$
\mathbf {P S N} _ {n} ^ {N} (t) = S _ {n} ^ {N} (t) \left\{R _ {n} ^ {N} (t) N [ d _ {1} ] - K N [ d _ {2} ] \right\},\tag{25.53}
$$

where 

$$
d _ {1} = \frac {1}{\sigma_ {n , N} \sqrt {T _ {n} - t}} \left[ \ln \left(\frac {R _ {n} ^ {N} (t)}{K}\right) + \frac {1}{2} \sigma_ {n, N} ^ {2} (T _ {n} - t) \right],\tag{25.54}
$$

$$
d _ {2} = d _ {1} - \sigma_ {n, N} \sqrt {T _ {n} - t}.\tag{25.55}
$$

The constant $\sigma _ { n , N }$ is known as the Black volatility . Given a market price for the swaption, the Black volatility implied by the Black formula is referred to as the implied Black volatility. 

As was the case with the Black formula for caps, the Black swaption formula has been used by the market for a long time, without any explicit coherent underlying model. Our task is thus to build an arbitrage free model with the property that the theoretical prices derived within the model have the structure of the Black-76 formula above. 

## 25.9 The Swap Market Models

From (25.52) it is clear that the natural choice of numeraire for swaptions is the accrual factor $S _ { n } ^ { N }$ and since the accrual factor has an intepretation as the value of a traded asset it is a bona fide choice of numeraire from the point of view of martingale measures. We now have the following simple but important result. 

Lemma 25.14 Denote the martingale measure for the numeraire $S _ { n } ^ { k }$ by $Q _ { n } ^ { k }$ Then the forward swap rate $R _ { n } ^ { k }$ is a $Q _ { n } ^ { k }$ -martingale. 

Proof This follows immediately from the fact that $R _ { n } ^ { k }$ is the value of a self financing portfolio (a long $\scriptstyle { T _ { n } }$ bond and a short $\scriptstyle { T _ { k } }$ bond), divided by the value of the self-financing portfolio $S _ { n } ^ { k }$ □ 

Thus the forward swap rate, like the LIBOR rates earlier, is a martingale under a suitable choice of numeraire, and the accrual factor plays the same role for swap market models as the bond prices did for the LIBOR models. The basic idea in the swaption market model which we will discuss below is then simply to model the forward swap rates $R _ { n } ^ { N }$ lognormally as GBM under the appropriate measures. 

Definition 25.15 Given the resettlement dates $T _ { 0 } , T _ { 1 } , T _ { N }$ , consider a fixed subset N of all positive integer pairs $^ { ( n , k ) }$ such that $0 \leq n < k \leq N$ . Consider furthermore, for each $( n , \mathbf { k } ) \in \mathcal { N } _ { : }$ , a deterministic function of time $\sigma _ { n , k } ( \cdot )$ ). A swap market model with the volatilities $\sigma _ { n , k }$ is then specified by assuming that the par swap rates have dynamics of the form 

$$
\mathrm{d} R _ {n} ^ {k} (t) = R _ {n} ^ {k} (t) \sigma_ {n, k} (t) \mathrm{d} W _ {n} ^ {k} (t), \quad (n, k) \in \mathcal {N},\tag{25.56}
$$

where $\smash { W _ { n } ^ { k } }$ is (possibly multidimensional) Wiener under $Q _ { n } ^ { k }$ 

Remark 25.9.1 Because of the interrelations between different par swap rates, we cannot model all possible swap rates $R _ { n } ^ { k }$ for $0 \leq \mathrm { n } < \mathrm { k } \leq \mathrm { N }$ simultaneously, so in a concrete model we have to restrict ourselves to modeling only a subset N of all par swap rates. In a model with N + 1 maturity dates we can only hope to model N independent swap rates, and typical choices of N are given by the following examples: 

A regular swap market model is specified by modeling, for a fixed N, the par swap rates $R _ { 0 } ^ { N } , R _ { 1 } ^ { N } , \ldots , R _ { n } ^ { N }$ i.e. 

$$
\mathcal {N} = \{(0, N), (1, N), \dots , (N - 1, N) \}.
$$

A reverse swap market model is specified by modeling, for a fixed N, the swap rates $\dot { R } _ { 0 } ^ { 1 } , R _ { 0 } ^ { 2 } , \dots , R _ { 0 } ^ { N }$ N i.e. 

$$
\mathcal {N} = \{(0, 1), (0, 2), \dots , (0, N) \}.
$$

25.10 Pricing Swaptions in t h e Swap Market Model Given a swap market model, the pricing of a $T _ { n } \mathrm { ~ x ~ } ( T _ { N } - T _ { n } )$ swaption is surprisingly trivial. Formula (24.6) immediately gives us the following pricing formula for the payer swaption (regardless of the specific form of the model): 

$$
\mathbf {P S N} _ {n} ^ {N} (t) = S _ {n} ^ {N} (t) \cdot E ^ {n, N} \left[ \max \left[ R _ {n} ^ {N} (T _ {n}) - \mathrm{K}; 0 \right] \mid \mathcal {F} _ {t} \right], \quad 0 \leq t \leq T _ {n}.\tag{25.57}
$$

Since $R _ { n } ^ { N }$ defined in (25.56), is just GBM we obtain 

$$
R _ {n} ^ {N} (T _ {n}) = R _ {n} ^ {N} (t) \cdot \mathrm{e} ^ {\int_ {t} ^ {T _ {n}} \sigma_ {n, N} (s) \mathrm{d} W _ {n} ^ {N} (s) - \frac {1}{2} \int_ {t} ^ {T _ {n}} \| \sigma_ {n, N} (s) \| ^ {2} \mathrm{d} s}.\tag{25.58}
$$

F'urthermore, since $\sigma _ { i }$ is assumed to be deterministic this implies that, conditional on $\mathcal { F } _ { t } , R _ { n } ^ { N } ( T _ { n } )$ is lognormal, i.e. we can write 

$$
L _ {i} (T _ {n}) = R _ {n} ^ {N} (t) \mathrm{e} ^ {Y _ {n} ^ {N} (t, T _ {n})},
$$

where ${ Y } _ { n } ^ { N } ( t , { T } _ { n } )$ is normally distributed with expected value 

$$
m _ {n} ^ {N} = - \frac {1}{2} \int_ {t} ^ {T _ {n}} \| \sigma_ {n, N} (s) \| ^ {2} d s,\tag{25.59}
$$

and variance 

$$
\Sigma_ {n, N} ^ {2} = \int_ {t} ^ {T _ {n}} \| \sigma_ {n, N} (s) \| ^ {2} d s.\tag{25.60}
$$

As for the LIBOR mode1;a simple calculation easily gives us the swaption pricing formula. 

Proposition 25.16 In the swap market model (25.56), the $T _ { n } \mathrm { x } \left( T _ { N } - T _ { n } \right)$ payer swaption price with strike K is given by 

$$
\mathbf {P S N} _ {n} ^ {N} (t) = S _ {n} ^ {N} (t) \left\{R _ {n} ^ {N} (t) N [ d _ {1} ] - K N [ d _ {2} ] \right\},\tag{25.61}
$$

where 

$$
\begin{array}{l} d _ {1} = \frac {1}{\Sigma_ {n , N}} \left[ \ln \left(\frac {R _ {n} ^ {N} (t)}{K}\right) + \frac {1}{2} \Sigma_ {n, N} ^ {2} \right], \\ d _ {2} = d _ {1} - \Sigma_ {n, N}. \end{array}\tag{25.62}
$$

(25.63) 

We thus see that each swaption price is given by a Black type formula. 

Remark 25.10.1 Sometimes it is more convenient working with a swap market model of the form 

$$
\mathrm{d} R _ {n} ^ {N} (t) = R _ {n} ^ {N} (t) \sigma_ {n, N} (t) \mathrm{d} W _ {n} ^ {N} (t),\tag{25.64}
$$

where $\sigma _ { n , N } ( t )$ t ) is a scalardeterministic function, $W _ { n } ^ { N }$ is a scalar @-Wiener process. Then the formulas above still hold if we replace $\| \sigma _ { n , N } \| ^ { 2 }$ 1I2by $\sigma _ { n , N } ^ { 2 }$ . We can also allow for correlation between the various Wiener processes, but this will not affect the swaption prices. Such a correlation will however affect the pricing of more complicated products. 

In this section, we have modeled each par swap rate $R _ { n } ^ { k }$ as GBM under it's own martingale measure $Q _ { n } ^ { k }$ and this led to the Black formula for swaptions. In order to price more exotic products we will typically have to resort to numerical methods like Monte Carlo, and then there is a need to specify the dynamics of the relevant par swap rates under a single martingale measure. This will be done in the next two sections. 

## 25.11 Drift Conditions for the Regular Swap Market Mode

In a regular swap market model, we model $R _ { n } ^ { N }$ for a fixed N and $0 \leq \mathrm { n } \leq \mathrm { N } - 1$ so the obvious choice of a common measure for all swap rates is $Q _ { N - 1 } ^ { N }$ which is nothing else (why?) than the $T _ { N } { \mathrm { - f o r w a r d } }$ measure $\hat { Q } ^ { T _ { N } }$ N. Our problem is to determine the various drift terms, and since this is somewhat messy it turns out to be convenient to have $\mathbb { T } _ { N + 1 }$ as the last payment date rather than $T _ { N }$ . We will thus model $R _ { 0 } ^ { N + 1 } , \dots , R _ { N } ^ { N + 1 }$ and our problem is to determine the drift terms of these par swap rates under the terminal measure $Q _ { N } ^ { N + 1 }$ 

Since the diffusion term of $R _ { m } ^ { N + 1 }$ will be the same under $Q _ { N } ^ { N + 1 }$ as under $Q _ { n } ^ { N + 1 }$ the $Q _ { N } ^ { N + 1 }$ dynamics of $R _ { n } ^ { N + 1 }$ are of the form 

$$
\mathrm{d} R _ {n} ^ {N + 1} = \mu_ {n} ^ {N + 1} R _ {n} ^ {N + 1} \mathrm{d} t + R _ {n} ^ {N + 1} \sigma_ {n, N + 1} \mathrm{d} W _ {N} ^ {N + 1},\tag{25.65}
$$

where $W _ { N } ^ { N + 1 }$ is a $Q _ { N } ^ { N + 1 }$ Wiener process, and our problem is to determine the drift term $\mu _ { n } ^ { N + 1 }$ 

The determination of the par swap drifts involves solving a backward linear difference equation, and for completeness' sake we now recall a general result for such equations. 

Proposition 25.17 The linear backward difference equation 

$$
x _ {n} = A _ {n + 1} x _ {n + 1} + b _ {n + 1}, \quad n = 0, \dots , N - 1,\tag{25.66}
$$

has the solution 

$$
x _ {n} = \left(\prod_ {j = n + 1} ^ {N} A _ {j}\right) x _ {N} + \sum_ {j = n} ^ {N - 1} \left(\prod_ {k = n + 1} ^ {j} A _ {k}\right) b _ {j + 1},\tag{25.67}
$$

with the convention $\begin{array} { r } { \prod _ { j = N + 1 } ^ { N } a _ { j } = 1 } \end{array}$ 

Proof Exercise for the reader. 

We may now state and prove the drift condition. 

Proposition 25.18 Under the terminal measure $Q _ { N } ^ { N + 1 }$ the $R _ { n } ^ { N + 1 }$ dynamics are of the form 

$$
\mathrm{d} R _ {n} ^ {N + 1} = \mu_ {n} ^ {N + 1} R _ {n} ^ {N + 1} \mathrm{d} t + R _ {n} ^ {N + 1} \sigma_ {n, N + 1} \mathrm{d} W _ {N} ^ {N + 1},\tag{25.68}
$$

where the drift term is given by 

$$
\mu_ {n} ^ {N + 1} = - \sigma_ {n, N + 1} \varphi_ {n},
$$

where 

$$
\varphi_ {n} = \sum_ {j = n} ^ {N - 1} \frac {Z _ {j + 1}}{Z _ {n}} \left[ \prod_ {k = n + 1} ^ {j} \left(1 + \alpha_ {k} R _ {k}\right) \right] \alpha_ {j + 1} R _ {j + 1} \sigma_ {j + 1} ^ {\star},\tag{25.69}
$$

and where $Z _ { n }$ is defined by 

$$
Z _ {n} = \frac {S _ {n}}{p _ {N + 1}}.\tag{25.70}
$$

Before going on with the proof we recall that we consider a regular swap market model for $R _ { 0 } ^ { N + 1 } , R _ { 1 } ^ { N + 1 } , \dots , R _ { N } ^ { N + 1 }$ and since the super index $\mathbf { N } + \mathbf { \Phi } _ { 1 }$ will be the same throughout the argument we henceforth suppress the superindex. 

<!-- === Source: MinerU_markdown_Arbitrage_Theory_in_Continuous_Time-Bjoerk_401_2122707855927779338.md (Page 401) === -->

Instead of $R _ { n } ^ { N + 1 } , ~ Q _ { n } ^ { N + 1 }$ and $\mu _ { n } ^ { N + 1 }$ we will thus write $R _ { n } , \ Q _ { n }$ , and $\mu _ { n }$ and similarly for all other terms. 

For easy reference we also recall the following relations: 

$$
R _ {n} = \frac {p _ {n} - p _ {N + 1}}{p _ {n}},\tag{25.71}
$$

$$
S _ {n} = \sum_ {i = n + 1} ^ {N + 1} \alpha_ {i} p _ {i},\tag{25.72}
$$

$$
\mathrm{d} R _ {n} = R _ {n} \sigma_ {n} \mathrm{d} W _ {n},\tag{25.73}
$$

where $W _ { n }$ is $Q _ { n } – \mathbf { W i e n e I }$ r. 

Proof We start by noticing that $\displaystyle { \cal S } _ { N } = p _ { N + 1 } , \mathrm { s o } { \cal Q } _ { N }$ is in fact the $T _ { N + 1 }$ l forward measure with numeraire $\pmb { p } \pmb { N } + \mathbf { 1 }$ 1 . From Proposition 24.4 we know that, with 

$$
L _ {n} (t) = \frac {Q _ {n}}{Q _ {N}}, \text {   on   } \mathcal {F} _ {t},
$$

we have 

$$
L _ {n} (t) = \gamma_ {n} Z _ {n} (t),
$$

where 

$$
Z _ {n} = \frac {S _ {n}}{p _ {N + 1}}, \quad \gamma_ {n} = Z _ {n} ^ {- 1} (0).\tag{25.74}
$$

Since $L _ { n }$ is a $Q _ { N }$ martingale it must have $Q _ { N }$ dynamics of the form 

$$
\mathrm{d} Z _ {n} = Z _ {n} \varphi_ {n} ^ {\star} \mathrm{d} W _ {N},\tag{25.75}
$$

so from (25.73), (25.65), and Girsanov's Theorem it follows that 

$$
\mu_ {n} = - \sigma_ {n} \varphi_ {n}.\tag{25.76}
$$

It thus remains to determine the process $\varphi _ { n }$ and to do this we must determine the $Z _ { n }$ dynamics from (25.74). From (25.72) we have 

$$
S _ {n} = S _ {n + 1} + \alpha_ {n + 1} p _ {n + 1},
$$

so from (25.74) we have 

$$
Z _ {n} = Z _ {n + 1} + \alpha_ {n + 1} \cdot \frac {p _ {n + 1}}{p _ {N + 1}}.\tag{25.77}
$$

From (25.71) we have 

$$
p _ {n + 1} = R _ {n + 1} S _ {n + 1} + p _ {N + 1},
$$

and plugging this into (25.77) gives us the recursion 

$$
Z _ {n} = Z _ {n + 1} \left(1 + \alpha_ {n + 1} R _ {n + 1}\right) + \alpha_ {n + 1}.\tag{25.78}
$$

From this formula, (25.65), and (25.75) we obtain the $Q _ { N }$ dynamics 

$$
\mathrm{d} Z _ {n} = Z _ {n + 1} \left(1 + \alpha_ {n + 1} R _ {n + 1}\right) \varphi_ {n + 1} ^ {\star} \mathrm{d} W _ {N} + Z _ {n + 1} \alpha_ {n + 1} R _ {n + 1} \sigma_ {n + 1} \mathrm{d} W _ {N},\tag{25.79}
$$

where we have used the fact that, under $Q _ { N } , Z _ { n }$ has zero drift. We thus have 

$$
\mathrm{d} Z _ {n} = Z _ {n} \frac {Z _ {n + 1}}{Z _ {n}} \left\{\left(1 + \alpha_ {n + 1} R _ {n + 1}\right) \varphi_ {n + 1} ^ {\star} + \alpha_ {n + 1} R _ {n + 1} \sigma_ {n + 1} \right\} \mathrm{d} W _ {N},\tag{25.80}
$$

so from (25.75) we obtain the following recursion for $\varphi _ { n }$ 

$$
\left\{ \begin{array}{l} \varphi_ {n} ^ {\star} = \frac {Z _ {n + 1}}{Z _ {n}} \left\{\left(1 + \alpha_ {n + 1} R _ {n + 1}\right) \varphi_ {n + 1} ^ {\star} + \alpha_ {n + 1} R _ {n + 1} \sigma_ {n + 1} \right\}, \\ \varphi_ {N} ^ {\star} = 0. \end{array} \right.\tag{25.81}
$$

From Proposition 25.17 we obtain the solution 

$$
\varphi_ {n} ^ {\star} = \sum_ {j = n} ^ {N - 1} \left(\prod_ {k = n + 1} ^ {j} a _ {k}\right) b _ {j + 1},
$$

where 

$$
a _ {k} = \frac {Z _ {k}}{Z _ {k - 1}} \left(1 + \alpha_ {k} R _ {k}\right), \quad b _ {j + 1} = \frac {Z _ {j + 1}}{Z _ {j}} \alpha_ {j + 1} R _ {j + 1} \sigma_ {j + 1}.
$$

A simple calculation gives us 

$$
\prod_ {k = n + 1} ^ {j} a _ {k} = \frac {Z _ {j}}{Z _ {n}} \prod_ {k = n + 1} ^ {j} (1 + \alpha_ {k} R _ {k})
$$

and we are done. 

## 25.12 Concluding Comment

It can be shown that, given a swap market model, the LIBOR rates will not be lognormal. Thus LIBOR market models and swap market models are in general incompatible.

## FORWARDS AND FUTURES

Consider a financial market of the type presented in the previous chapter, with an underlying factor process X , and with a (possibly stochastic) short rate r. (If r is stochastic we include it, for brevity of notation, as one component of X.) We assume that the market is arbitrage free, and that pricing is done under some fixed risk neutral martingale measure Q (with, as usual, B as numeraire). 

Let us now consider a fixed simple T-claim y, i.e. a claim of the form ${ \mathcal { Y } } = \Psi ( X _ { T } )$ , and assume that we are standing at time t. If we buy Y and pay today, i.e. at time t, then we know that the arbitrage free price is given by 

$$
\Pi (t; \mathcal {Y}) = G (t, X _ {t}; T, \mathcal {Y}),\tag{26.1}
$$

where the pricing function G is given by 

$$
G (t, x; T, \mathcal {Y}) = E _ {t, x} ^ {Q} \left[ \mathcal {Y} \cdot \exp \left\{- \int_ {t} ^ {T} r (s) \mathrm{d} s \right\} \right],\tag{26.2}
$$

and the payment streams are as follows: 

1. At time t we pay n ( t ; y ) to the underwriter of the contract. 

2. At time T we receive y from the underwriter. 

There are two extremely common variations of this type of contract, namely forwards and futures. Both these contracts have the same claim y as their underlying object, but they differ from our standard contract above by the way in which payments are made. 

## 26.1 Forward Contracts

We will start with the conceptually easiest contract, which is the forward contract. This is an agreement between two parties to buy or sell a certain underlying claim at a fixed time T in the future. The difference between a forward contract and our standard claims studied so far is that for a forward contract all payments are made at time T. To be more precise we give a definition. 

Definition 26.1 Let y be a contingent T-claim. A forward contract on y , contracted at t, with time of delivery T, and with the forward price f (t; T, Y), is defined by the following payment scheme: 

The holder of the forward contract receives, at time T, the stochastic amount Y from the underwriter. 

The holder of the contract pays, at time T, the amount $f ( t ,  { \mathrm { T } } ,  { \mathcal { V } } )$ to the underwriter. 

The forward price $f ( t , T , \mathcal { V } )$ is determined at time t. 

The forward price $f ( t , \mathrm { T } , \mathfrak { V } )$ is determined i n such a way that the price of the forward contract equals zero, at the time t when the contract is made. 

Forward markets are typically not standardized, so forward contracts are usually traded as OTC ("over the counter") instruments. Note that even if the value of a specific forward contract equals zero at the time t of writing the contract, it will typically have a nonzero market value which varies stochastically in the time interval $[ t \mathcal { T } ]$ 

Our immediate project is to give a mathematical formalization of the definition above, and to derive a theoretical expression for the forward price process $f ( t , \mathrm { T } , \mathcal { Y } )$ . This turns out to be quite simple, since the forward contract itself is a contingent T-claim $\xi ,$ <, defined by 

$$
\xi = \mathcal {Y} - f (t; T, \mathcal {Y}).
$$

We are thus led to the following mathematical definition of the forward price process. 

Definition 26.2 Let y be a contingent T-claim as above. By the forward price process we mean a process $f ( t , \mathbf { T } , \mathfrak { V } )$ of the form $f ( t ; \dot { T } , \mathcal { y } ) { = } f ( t , X _ { t } ; \bar { \mathrm { T } } , \mathcal { y } )$ where f is some determinstic function, with the property that 

$$
\Pi (t; \mathcal {Y} - f (t, X _ {t}; T, \mathcal {Y})) = 0.\tag{26.3}
$$

Writing the forward price as $\mathbf { f } \left( t , { { X } _ { t } } ; { T } , \mathcal { Y } \right)$ formalizes the fact that the forward price is determined at t , given the information that is available at that time. 

We now have the following basic formula for the forward price process. 

Proposition 26.3 The forward price process is given by any of the following expressions: 

$$
f (t; T, \mathcal {Y}) = \frac {\Pi (t ; \mathcal {Y})}{p (t , T)},\tag{26.4}
$$

$$
f (t; T, \mathcal {Y}) = f (t, X _ {t}; T, \mathcal {Y}),\tag{26.5}
$$

where 

$$
f (t, x; T, \mathcal {Y}) = \frac {1}{p (t , T)} E _ {t, x} ^ {Q} \left[ \mathcal {Y} \cdot \exp \left\{- \int_ {t} ^ {T} r (s) \mathrm{d} s \right\} \right],\tag{26.6}
$$

$$
f (t, x; T, \mathcal {Y}) = E _ {t, x} ^ {T} [ \mathcal {Y} ].\tag{26.7}
$$

Proof Using (26.3) and risk neutral valuation we immediately have the following identities, where we write $\operatorname { f } \left( t , x \right)$ instead of $f ( t , \mathrm { x ; T } , \mathcal { V } )$ 

$$
\begin{array}{l} 0 = \Pi (t; \mathcal {Y} - f (t, X _ {t})) = E _ {t, X _ {t}} ^ {Q} \left[ [ \mathcal {Y} - f (t, X _ {t}) ] \cdot \exp \left\{- \int_ {t} ^ {T} r (s) \mathrm{d} s \right\} \right] \\ \text {互} = E _ {t, X _ {t}} ^ {Q} \left[ \mathcal {Y} \cdot \exp \left\{- \int_ {t} ^ {T} r (s) \mathrm{d} s \right\} \right] - E _ {t, X _ {t}} ^ {Q} \left[ f (t, X _ {t}). \exp \left\{- \int_ {t} ^ {T} r (s) \mathrm{d} s \right\} \right] \\ = \Pi (t; \mathcal {Y}) - f (t, X _ {t}) E _ {t, X _ {t}} ^ {Q} \left[ \exp \left\{- \int_ {t} ^ {T} r (s) \mathrm{d} s \right\} \right] \\ = \Pi (t; \mathcal {Y}) - f (t, X _ {t}) p (t, T). \end{array}
$$

This immediately gives us (26.4)-(26.6). The relation (26.7) then follows from (26.6). □ 

Note that when dealing with forward contracts there is some risk of conceptual confusion. If we fix t, T and , and let s be a fixed point in time with $\mathfrak { t } \le \mathfrak { s } \le T$ 2 then there will be two different prices. 

1. The forward price $\mathbf { f } \left( \pmb { \mathscr { s } } ; \mathrm { T } , \mathcal { y } \right)$ which is paid t o the underwriter a t time T for a forward contract made at time s. 

2. The (spot) price, a t time s , of a fixed forward contract, entered a t time t, and with time T of delivery. This spot price is easily seen to be equal to 

$$
\Pi (s; \mathcal {Y}) - p (s, T) f (t; T, \mathcal {Y}).
$$

## 26.2 Futures Contracts

A futures contract is very much like a forward contract in the sense that it is an agreement between two parties to buy or sell a certain claim at a prespecified the two contracts lies in :ive a ver ,bal defini. tion of the futures contract. 

Definition 26.4 Let y be a contingent T-claim. A futures contract on ${ \mathfrak { p } } ,$ with time of delivery $\mathbf { T } ,$ is a financial asset with the following properties: 

(i) At every point of time t with $0 \leq \mathfrak { t } \leq \mathrm { T }$ , there k s t s in the market a quoted object $\bar { F } ( \bar { t } ; \mathrm { T } , \mathcal { y } )$ , lcnown as the futures price for Y at t, for delivery at T. 

(ii) At the time T of delivery, the holder of the contract pays $F ( T ; \mathrm { T } , \mathcal { V } )$ and receives the claim y . 

(iiz) During a n arbitrary time interval (s, t] the holder of the contract receives the amount $F ( t ; \mathrm { T } , \dot { \boldsymbol { y } } ) - F ( s ; \mathrm { T } , \mathrm { Y } )$ 

(zv) The spot price, at any time t prior to delivery, of obtaining the futures contract, is by definition equal to zero. 

A rough way of thinking about a futures contract is to regard it as a forward contract where the payments are made continuously in time in the way described above, rather than all payments being made at time T. As the forward price increased, you would then get richer, and as the forward price decreased you would lose money. The reason that this way of looking at the futures contract is not entirely correct is the fact that if we start with a standard forward contract, with its associated forward price process f , and then introduce the above payment scheme over time, this will (through supply and demand) affect the original forward price process, so generically we will expect the futures price process F to be different from the forward price process f. The payment schedule above is known as "marking to market"; it is organized in such a way that the holder of a futures position, be it short or long, is required to keep a certain amount of money with the broker as a safety margin against default. 

Futures contracts, as opposed to forward contracts, are traded in a standardized manner at an exchange. The volumes in which futures are traded over the world are astronomical, and one of the reasons for this is that on many markets it is difficult to trade (or hedge) directly in the underlying object. A typical example is the commodity market, where you actually have to deliver the traded object (tons of copper, timber, or ripening grapes), and thus are not allowed to go short. In these markets, the futures contract is a convenient financial instrument which does not force you to physically deliver the underlying object, while still making it possible for you to hedge (or speculate) against the underlying object. 

We now note some properties of the futures contract: 

a From (ii) and (iv) above it is clear that we must have 

$$
F (T; T, \mathcal {Y}) = \mathcal {Y}.\tag{26.8}
$$

Thus there is really no economic reason to actually deliver either the underlying claim or the payment at time T. This is also an empirical fact; the vast majority of all futures contracts are closed before the time of delivery. 

If you enter a futures contract at time t with a corresponding futures price $F ( t ; \mathrm { T } , \mathcal { V } )$ , this does not mean that you are obliged to deliver y at time T at the price $F ( t ; T , \mathcal { y } )$ . The only contractual obligation is the payment stream defined above. 

a The name futures price is therefore somewhat unfortunate from a linguistic point of view. If today's futures price is given by $F ( t ; \mathrm { T } , \mathcal { I } )$ (with $\mathbf { t } < \mathbf { T } )$ this does not mean that anyone will ever pay the amount $F ( t ; \mathrm { T } , \mathcal { \boldsymbol { y } } )$ in order to obtain some asset. It would perhaps be more clear to refer to $\dot { F } ( t ; \mathrm { T } , \mathcal { I } )$ as the futures quotation. 

Since, by definition, the spot price of a futures contract equals zero, there is no cost or gain of entering or closing a futures contract. 

If the reader thinks that a futures contract conceptually is a somewhat complicated object, then the author is inclined to agree. 

# FUTURES CONTRACTS

We now turn to the mathematical formalization of the futures contract, and it should by now be clear that the natural model for a futures contract is an asset with dividends. 

Definition 26.5 The futures contract on an underlying T-claim y is a fin ancial asset with a price process II ( t ) and a dividend process D ( t ) satisfying the following conditions: 

$$
D (t) = F (t; T, \mathcal {Y}).\tag{26.9}
$$

$$
F (T; T, \mathcal {Y}) = \mathcal {Y}.\tag{26.10}
$$

$$
\dot {\Pi} (t) = 0, \forall t \leq T.\tag{26.11}
$$

It now remains to investigate what the futures price process looks like. This turns out to be quite simple, and we can now prove the main result of the section. 

Proposition 26.6 Let y be a given contingent T-claim, and assume that market prices are obtained from the jixed risk neutral martingale measure Q. Then the following hold: 

a The futures price process is given by 

$$
F (t; T, \mathcal {Y}) = E _ {t, X _ {t}} ^ {Q} [ \mathcal {Y} ].\tag{26.12}
$$

a If the short rate is deterministic, then the forward and the futures price processes coincide, and we have 

$$
f (t; T, \mathcal {Y}) = F (t; T, \mathcal {Y}) = E _ {t, X _ {t}} ^ {Q} [ \mathcal {Y} ].\tag{26.13}
$$

Proof From Proposition 16.14, it follows that the discounted gains process 

$$
G ^ {Z} (t) = \frac {\Pi (t)}{B _ {t}} + \int_ {0} ^ {t} \frac {1}{B _ {s}} \mathrm{d} F (s; T, \mathcal {Y})
$$

has the representation 

$$
\mathrm{d} G _ {t} ^ {Z} = h _ {t} \mathrm{d} W _ {t}
$$

for some adapted process h. In our case we furthermore have $\Pi ( t ) { = } 0$ for all t , so we obtain the representation 

$$
\frac {1}{B _ {t}} \mathrm{d} F (t; T, \mathcal {Y}) = h _ {t} \mathrm{d} W _ {t}.
$$

Multiplying by $B _ { t }$ on both sides we get 

$$
\mathrm{d} F (t; T, \mathcal {Y}) = B _ {t} h _ {t} \mathrm{d} W _ {t},
$$

which implies that $F ( t ; T , \mathcal { V } )$ is a Q-martingale. Using the martingale property, the fact that we are in a Markovian framework (see Lemma 5.9), and (26.10) we obtain 

$$
F (t; T, \mathcal {Y}) = E _ {t, X _ {t}} ^ {Q} [ F (T; T, \mathcal {Y}) ] = E _ {t, X _ {t}} ^ {Q} [ \mathcal {Y} ],
$$

# FORWARDS AND FUTURES

which proves the first part of the assertion. The second part follows from the fact that $Q ^ { \mathrm { T } } = \mathbf { Q }$ when the short rate is deterministic (see Lemma 24.9).

## Appendix A

## MEASURE AND INTEGRATION*

The purpose of this appendix is to give an introduction to measure theory and to the associated integration theory on general measure spaces. 

## A.l Sets and Mappings

Let X be an arbitrary set. We then say that X is finite if it contains only finitely many elements. If X is not finite, we say that it is infinite. We will use the notation ${ \bf f } : { \bf X }  { \bf Y }$ to denote a function (or "mapping") f which takes values in Y and which has domain X. If we apply the f to an element $\mathbf { x } \in \mathbf { X }$ we denote the function value by f (x). 

Definition A . l Let X and Y be sets and let 

$$
\mathrm{f}: X \to Y
$$

be a given mapping. 

1. The mapping f is injective i i for all x and z i n X it holds that 

$$
x \neq z \Rightarrow f (x) \neq f (z).
$$

2. The mapping f is surjective i;f, for ally $\in \mathrm { Y }$ , there exists an $\mathbf { \mu } _ { \mathbf { X } } \in \mathbf { X }$ such that 

$$
\mathrm{Y} = f (x).
$$

upping f is bijective if it is both injective and surjective 

4. The image of X under f , is denoted by Im(f), and defined by 

$$
\operatorname{Im} (f) = \{f (x); x \in X \}.
$$

5. For any set $\mathbf { B } \subseteq Y$ , the inverse image or pullback of B under f, is denoted by $f ^ { - 1 } ( B )$ and defined by 

$$
f ^ {- 1} (B) = \{x; f (x) \in \mathrm{B}).
$$

We also say that B is lifted $t o \mathbf { f } ^ { - 1 } ( B )$ 

6. In particular, for every $y \in Y$ we write 

$$
f ^ {- 1} (y) = \{x; f (x) = y \}.
$$

7. For any set $\mathbf { A } \subseteq X$ the direct image of B under f is denoted by $f ( \mathbf { A } )$ and defined by 

$$
f (A) = \{f (x); x \in A \}.
$$

Note that the inverse image of a set always exists (although it could be the empty set) even if the function f does not have an inverse. For our purposes the inverse image concept is much more important than the direct image. The following very useful result shows that the set algebraic operations are preserved under the inverse image. 

Proposition A.2 The following relations always hold: 

1. For any $\mathbf { A } , \mathbf { B } \subseteq \mathbf { Y }$ we have 

$$
f ^ {- 1} (A n B) = f ^ {- 1} (A) \cap f ^ {- 1} (B).
$$

2. For any $\mathbf { A } , B \subseteq \mathrm { Y }$ we have 

$$
f ^ {- 1} (A \cup B) = f ^ {- 1} (A) \cup f ^ {- 1} (B).
$$

3. For any $B \subseteq Y$ we have 

$$
\mathrm{f} ^ {- 1} (\mathrm{B} ^ {\mathrm{c}}) = \left[ \mathrm{f} ^ {- 1} (\mathrm{B}) \right] ^ {\mathrm{c}}
$$

where denotes the complement. 

4. For any indexed collection $\{ \boldsymbol { B } _ { \boldsymbol { \gamma } } \} _ { \boldsymbol { \gamma } \in \Gamma }$ of sets i n Y we have 

$$
f ^ {- 1} \left(\bigcap_ {\gamma \in \Gamma} B _ {\gamma}\right) = \bigcap_ {\gamma \in \Gamma} f ^ {- 1} (B _ {\gamma}).
$$

5. For any indexed collection $\{ B _ { \gamma } \} _ { \gamma \in \Gamma }$ of sets i n Y we have 

$$
f ^ {- 1} \left(\bigcup_ {\gamma \in \Gamma} B _ {\gamma}\right) = \bigcup_ {\gamma \in \Gamma} f ^ {- 1} (B _ {\gamma}).
$$

Proof We leave the proof to the reader. 

We define the set of natural numbers as the set $\Nu = \{ 1 , 2 , \ldots \}$ , and the set of integers $Z$ as $Z = \{ 0 , \pm 1 , \pm 2 , \ldots \}$ . Using N we can give a name to the "smallest" type of infinite set. 

Definition A.3 A n infinite set X is countable if there exists a bijection 

$$
f: N \to X.
$$

If X is infinite but not countable, it is said to be uncountable. 

Note that in our definition a countable set is always infinite. The intuitive interpretation of this is that a countable set has "as many" elements as N, whereas an uncountable set has "more" elements than N. If X is countable we may, for each $\mathbf { n } \in \mathbf { N }$ define $\pmb { x _ { n } } \in \mathrm { X }$ by ${ x _ { n } = \operatorname { f } \left( n \right) }$ . Since f is a bijection we can thus write X as 

$$
X = \{x _ {1}, x _ {2}, x _ {3}, \dots \},
$$

so we see that in this sense we can really count off the elements in X , one-by-one. 

A countable set is thus an infinite set, but in a sense it is "almost finite", and thus very easy and nice to handle. In mathematics in general and in particular in probability theory, the difference between countable and uncountable sets is crucial, and therefore it is important to be able to tell if a set is countable or not. The following result is a good start in that direction. 

Proposition A.4 The set Q of rational numbers is countable. 

Proof It is enough to show that the set $Q _ { + }$ of positive rational numbers is countable, and we do this by first representing each rational number ${ \pmb p } / { \pmb q }$ by the integer lattice point $( \mathbf { p } , \mathbf { q } ) \in \mathbf { R } ^ { 2 }$ . We now prove that this set of integer lattice points is countable by simply presenting a scheme for counting them. 

The scheme begins with $( 1 , 1 ) , ( { \bar { 2 , 1 } } ) , ( 1 , 2 ) , ( 1 , 3 ) , ( 2 , 2 ) , ( 3 , 1 ) , ( 4 , 1 ) , ( 3 , 2 )$ , and if the reader draws a two-dimensional graph of this scheme, she will easily see how to continue. 

This simple idea can be extended considerably. 

Proposition A.5 Assume that we give a countable family $\{ X _ { n } \} _ { i = 1 } ^ { \infty }$ l of sets, where each set $X _ { n }$ is countable. Then the union $\textstyle \bigcup _ { i = 1 } ^ { \infty } { \bar { X } } _ { n }$ is countable. 

Proof Because of the countability assumption, the set $X _ { i }$ can be written as $\{ x _ { i 1 } , x _ { i 2 } , x _ { i 3 } , \ldots \}$ , SO the set $X _ { i }$ can be bijectively mapped into the integer lattice points of the form $( i , 1 ) , ( i , 2 ) , ( i , 3 ) , \ldots .$ . Thus the union $\cup _ { i = 1 } ^ { \infty } X _ { n }$ can be mapped bijectively onto the entire set of positive integer lattice points in $\mathbf { R } ^ { 2 }$ and we have already proved that this set is countable. □ 

The most important example of an uncountable set is the set of real numbers. 

Proposition A.6 The set R of real numbers is uncountable. 

Proof Omitted. 

## A.2 Measures and Sigma Algebras

Let X be a set and let us denote the class of all subsets of X by ${ \bf 2 ^ { X } }$ . More formally we thus see that $2 ^ { X }$ , commonly known as the power set of X , is a set, the elements of which are subsets of X . 

We now want to formalize the idea of a mass distribution on X , and the reader may think of a large plate (the set X ) with mashed potatoes on it. For every subset $\mathbf { A } \subseteq \mathbf { X }$ we would now like to define the nonnegative real number $\mu ( \mathrm { A } )$ as "the amount of mashed potatoes which lies on the set $\mathbf { A } "$ or "the measure of $\mathbf { A } "$ . However, when one tries to formalize this intuitively simple notion, one encounters technical problems, and the main problem is the fact that in the generic situation, there exist subsets $\mathbf { A } \subseteq \mathbf { X }$ which axe so "nasty" that it is mathematically impossible to define $\mu ( A )$ . Typically we are therefore forced to define the measure $\mu ( A )$ only for certain "nice" subsets $\mathbf A \subseteq \mathbf X$ . These "nice<sup>7</sup>' sets are called "measurable sets", and the technical concept needed is that of a sigma-algebra (or o-algebra). In order to define this concept, let 3 be a family of subsets of $\mathbf { X } , \mathbf { i } . \mathbf { e } . 3 \subseteq \mathbf { \bar { 2 } } ^ { X }$

One of the most striking properties of the integral concept defined above is the surprising ease with which it handles convergence problems. The three basic results are as follows. 

Theorem A.21 (The Fatou Lemma) Let $\left\{ f _ { n } \right\} _ { n = 1 } ^ { \infty }$ be a sequence of measurable functions such that 

$$
f _ {n} \geq 0, \quad n = 1, 2, \dots
$$

and 

$$
\lim _ {n \rightarrow \infty} f _ {n} (x) = f (x), \forall x E X,
$$

for some limit function f. Then 

$$
\int_ {X} f (x) \mathrm{d} \mu (x) \leq \liminf _ {n} \int_ {X} f _ {n} (x) \mathrm{d} \mu (x).
$$

Theorem A.22 (Monotone Convergence) Let $\left\{ f _ { n } \right\} _ { n = 1 } ^ { \infty }$ be a sequence of measurable functions such that 

1. The sequence is nonnegative, i.e. 

$$
f _ {n} \geq 0, \quad n = 1, 2, \dots
$$

2. The sequence is increasing, i.e. for all x we have 

$$
f _ {1} (x) \leq f _ {2} (x) \leq \dots \leq f _ {n} (x) \leq f _ {n + 1} (x) \leq \dots .
$$

Then, defining the function f by 

$$
f (x) = \lim _ {n} f _ {n} (x),
$$

it holds that 

$$
\int_ {X} f (x) \mathrm{d} \mu (x) = \lim _ {n} \int_ {X} f _ {n} (x) \mathrm{d} \mu (x).
$$

Theorem A.23 (The Lebesgue Dominated Convergence Theorem) Let $\left\{ f _ { n } \right\} _ { n = 1 } ^ { \infty }$ be a sequence of measurable functions such that 

$$
f _ {n} (x) \rightarrow f (x)
$$

for some limit function f . Suppose that there exists a nonnegative function $g \in { \cal L } ^ { 1 }$ such that, 

$$
\left| f _ {n} (x) \right| \leq g (x), \quad \forall n, \forall x \in X.
$$

Then 

$$
\int_ {X} f (x) \mathrm{d} \mu (x) = \lim _ {n} \int_ {X} f _ {n} (x) \mathrm{d} \mu (x).
$$

## A.4 Sigma- Algebras and Partitions

The purpose of this section is to give some more intuition for the measurability concept for functions. We will do this by considering the simplest case of a sigma-algebra, namely when it is generated by a partition. 

Definition A.24 A partition P of the space X is a finite collection of sets $\{ A _ { 1 } , A _ { 2 } , \ldots , A , )$ such that 

1. The sets cover X , i. e. 

$$
\bigcup_ {i = 1} ^ {n} A _ {i} = X,
$$

2. The sets are disjoint, i.e. 

$$
i \neq j \Rightarrow A _ {i} \cap A _ {j} = \emptyset .
$$

The sets $A _ { 1 } , \ldots , A _ $ , are called the components of P , and the sigma-algebm consisting of all possible unions (including the empty set) of the components i n P is denoted by $\sigma \left( P \right)$ . This sigma-algebra is called the sigma-algebra generated by P . 

We now have a result which shows (in this restricted setting) what measurability for a function "really means". 

Proposition A.25 Let P be a given partition of X . A function $f : X \to R$ is $\sigma \left( \mathcal { P } \right)$ -measurable if and only iff is constant on each component of P . 

Proof First assume that f is measurable, and consider a fixed but arbitrarily chosen real number y. Since f is measurable we know that $f ^ { - 1 } ( y )$ is in $o \left( P \right)$ so it is a union of some of the components of P . If the union is nonempty thi means precisely that $\mathbf { f } = y$ on that union, so in particular it takes the constant value y on all components in the union. The converse is trivial. □ 

The sigma-algebras that we are going to consider later on in the text, are in general not generated by partitions. They are typically much more complicated, so the proposition above is of little "practical" interest. The point of the discussion concerning partitions is instead that when you informally think about sigma-algebras, it is very fruitful to have this simple case at the back of your head. 

As an example, we see directly from Proposition A.25 why we must restrict ourselves to integrating measurable functions only. The problem with a nonmeasurable function is that the function is varying too wildly compared with the fine structure of the sigma-algebra. In particular this implies that a nonmeasurable function cannot be well approximated by simple functions. 

It is also very instructive to see exactly what goes wrong when we try to integrate nonmeasurable functions. Even for a nonmeasurable function f we can of course in principle define the integral by (A.4), but this integral will not have the nice properties in Proposition A.20. See the exercises for concrete examples.

Let p be a real number with $I \leq { \mathsf { p } } < \infty$ . We define the function class $\operatorname { L } ^ { \mathrm { p } } \left( X , { \mathcal { F } } , \mu \right)$ as the class of measurable functions f such that
